sections.heading: Where This Series Begins
pulls: The sermon does not ask whether you are better than other men. It asks whether your righteousness surpasses the best men alive — and it does not.
paras: Every man who has felt the dust knows the quiet, exhausting question of religion: am I good enough? He measures himself against the man beside him, against the standard in his head, against the law as he understands it, and on a good week he feels he is getting somewhere. The Sermon on the Mount exists, in part, to take that good week away from him. Jesus climbs a mountain, sits down like a rabbi about to teach, and proceeds to dismantle every confidence a man has ever built in his own righteousness — not to leave him in ruins, but to drive him to the only righteousness that can actually save.

That is why this study begins where it does. Before you walk through anger and lust and money and anxiety, you have to hear the verse that governs all of it: “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.” This is the lens for all twelve weeks. The sermon is not a self-improvement plan handed to capable men. It is a mountain of demand set deliberately too high, so that a man stops trusting his own climbing and looks up to the One who already stands at the summit in his place.

sections.heading: A Mirror, Not a Ladder
paras: The mistake that ruins a man before he begins is this: he reads the Sermon on the Mount as a ladder he is supposed to climb. Try harder, get angry less, lust less, give more, worry less — climb your way up to the kingdom. But Jesus has already told you the top rung is higher than the most religious men who ever lived, and you have never once reached their rung. The ladder reading ends in either despair or self-deception, and the Pharisee chose self-deception. He lowered the law until he could keep it, congratulated himself, and missed the kingdom entirely.

The sermon is not a ladder. It is a mirror. Its purpose is to show you, with merciless clarity, the true state of your heart — and then to send you looking away from yourself for a righteousness you cannot manufacture. The man who reads it as a mirror is not crushed for no reason; he is being driven somewhere. Every demand he cannot meet is an arrow pointing to the One who met them all. Conviction, in this sermon, is never the destination. It is the road to Christ.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Bar Is Set Where You Cannot Reach
paras: Notice how high Jesus sets the bar in the very first paragraphs. He says he did not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it, and that not one stroke of a letter will pass away. Then he says your righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. He is not lowering the standard to make it manageable; he is raising it past the reach of the most disciplined men in Israel. And before the chapter ends he will push it further still — the law does not stop at murder but reaches anger, does not stop at adultery but reaches the lustful glance.

This is deliberate, and it is mercy. A bar a man can clear leaves him trusting himself. A bar no man can clear sends him looking for help. The dust says, just do a little better and you will be fine. The Word says the standard is perfection, and you have already failed it, and your only hope is a righteousness from outside yourself. The height of the bar is not cruelty. It is the kindness that empties a man’s hands so they are free to receive.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Righteousness You Need Is a Gift, Not a Wage
paras: If the righteousness that enters the kingdom must surpass the Pharisees’, and no man’s does, then either no one is saved or the righteousness must come from somewhere other than the man. This is the hinge of the whole gospel and the secret of the whole sermon. Paul, who once was a Pharisee with a righteousness he was proud of, came to count it all as loss — he no longer wanted “a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law,” but “the righteousness which is from God by faith,” found only in Christ. The very thing the Sermon on the Mount demands and you cannot produce, God provides as a gift in his Son.

This is what makes the surpassing righteousness good news instead of a death sentence. Jesus kept the sermon perfectly — every command, in thought and word and deed — and that flawless righteousness is credited to the man who trusts him. So when you stand before God, you are not offering him your best week. You are clothed in the righteousness of Christ, which exceeds the scribes and Pharisees infinitely, because it is the righteousness of God himself. The kingdom opens not to the man who climbed but to the man who was clothed.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Blessed Are the Bankrupt
paras: This is why the sermon opens the way it does — not with “blessed are the accomplished” but with “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.” Before a single command is given, Jesus pronounces blessing on the man who knows he is spiritually bankrupt. The kingdom is not entered by the man who brings his righteousness; it is given to the man who knows he has none to bring. Poverty of spirit is not the first rung of the ladder. It is the abandonment of the ladder altogether.

This is deep relief for a man in the dust. The very emptiness you are ashamed of — the failure, the inability, the soul clinging to the floor — is the doorway. Jesus does not bless the man who has it together. He blesses the man who has come to the end of himself. The whole sermon will press you toward that end, again and again, because the kingdom belongs to the bankrupt who look to Christ, and not to the rich who look to themselves.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to a Borrowed Righteousness
paras: Psalm 119:25 anchors this whole series: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). This is how revival begins. It does not begin with you scaling the mountain by willpower. It begins with the Word showing you that the summit is beyond you — and then pointing you to the One who already stands there with arms open. The clinging is real. Some mornings the sense of failure is all you feel. But your entrance to the kingdom was never going to be your own righteousness. It was always going to be his.

So this week you are not trying to start obeying the sermon better. You are learning to read it rightly — as a mirror that drives you to Christ, not a ladder that leaves you in the dust. When the demands of the coming weeks expose you, do not despair and do not pretend. Let the exposure send you, every time, to the righteousness that surpasses, the righteousness of Christ, given to men who have none of their own.

stations.verse: For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
stations.question: If the righteousness that enters the kingdom must surpass the best men alive, whose righteousness have I secretly been counting on — mine, or Christ’s?
stations.gloss: righteousness, the state of being right before God
stations.live: When the sermon exposes you this week, do not reach for a better performance. Reach for the standing that is already yours in Christ — a righteousness from God, not from you.
body: Dikaiosynē is the standing a man must have to be accepted by God — not merely good behavior, but a right standing before the Judge. Jesus says the standing you need must surpass the most religious men who ever lived. This is precisely the word Paul uses when he says a righteousness from God has been revealed apart from the law, given through faith in Christ. The righteousness the sermon demands of you is the righteousness the gospel gives to you.

stations.verse: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
stations.question: The kingdom is promised to the spiritually bankrupt. Do I come to God admitting I have nothing to bring, or still hoping to impress him with something?
stations.gloss: poor, destitute, a beggar with nothing
stations.live: Stop trying to come to God with full hands. Come as the beggar you are — and receive the kingdom he gives to the empty.
body: Ptōchos does not mean merely having little; it means having nothing — the word for a beggar crouched with his hand out, utterly dependent on what another gives. Jesus blesses the man who is spiritually that poor, who knows he brings nothing to the transaction. The kingdom is not a wage paid to the rich in spirit; it is a gift handed to the beggar who admits he is empty.

stations.verse: Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
stations.question: Jesus came to fulfill the law I could never keep. How does it change my week to know he kept it perfectly in my place?
stations.gloss: to fulfill, to complete, to fill up to the full
stations.live: When the law accuses you this week, point it to Christ, who fulfilled it. Its every demand has already been met by the One you belong to.
body: Plēroō means to bring a thing to its full, intended completion. Jesus did not come to lower the law or set it aside; he came to fill it full — to obey it perfectly, embody it entirely, and accomplish everything it pointed toward. Every command you have broken, he kept. The law you could not fulfill, he fulfilled, and his fulfillment is reckoned to those who are his.

stations.verse: Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith,
stations.question: Paul threw away his own righteousness to gain Christ’s. What righteousness of my own am I still clinging to that I need to count as loss?
stations.gloss: loss, damage, the thing written off
stations.live: Name the line in your own ledger you still count as gain before God — the churchgoing, the decency, the comparison. Write it off this week, and take Christ in its place.
body: Zēmia is a ledger word. It is what goes in the loss column. Luke uses it for the loss of a ship and her cargo in the storm off Crete — goods a man once counted as his, gone to the bottom. Paul takes his whole religious record — the pedigree, the zeal, the blameless law-keeping — and moves it from the gain column to the loss column. Not because it was nothing, but because next to Christ it could not stay on the books. A man does not add Christ to his record. He writes the record off and takes Christ instead.

stations.verse: Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin. But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction,
stations.question: No one is justified by keeping the law. Why do I keep trying to earn a standing the law was never able to give me?

stations.verse: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.
stations.question: Jesus blesses the man who hungers for a righteousness he does not have. Do I hunger for Christ’s righteousness, or am I full on my own?
stations.gloss: to fill, to satisfy completely, to feed to the full
stations.live: Bring your hunger to Christ this week, not your fullness. He satisfies the starving, not the self-sufficient.
body: Chortazō was used for feeding until completely full, and for satisfying a starving man until he could eat no more. Jesus promises that the one who hungers and thirsts for righteousness will not be given a scrap but will be filled to satisfaction. The man who knows he lacks righteousness and longs for it will find himself filled — not by his own striving, but by the righteousness Christ supplies.

stations.verse: For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
stations.question: In Christ I become the very righteousness of God. How would my week look different if I truly carried myself as a man already counted righteous in him?

stations.verse: For being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn’t subject themselves to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
stations.question: Where am I still trying to establish my own righteousness instead of submitting to the righteousness God gives in Christ?

stations.verse: There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!
stations.question: If there is no other name and no other righteousness that saves, what other hope have I quietly been keeping in reserve?
pulls: The sermon shows you the righteousness you must have and do not. Christ is the righteousness you must have and cannot earn.

practices.title: NAME WHOSE RIGHTEOUSNESS YOU ARE TRUSTING
practices.body: Most men have never consciously answered the most important question of their lives: when you stand before God, whose righteousness are you counting on? This week, answer it out loud. Be honest about the ways you quietly trust your own — your church attendance, your decency, your better-than-that-guy comparisons. Write down the righteousness you have been leaning on, then write across it the truth of Philippians 3: “not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith.” You cannot rest in Christ’s righteousness while still betting on your own.

practices.title: READ THE SERMON AS A MIRROR, NOT A LADDER
practices.body: As you begin this study, set your expectation correctly. You are not here to be graded and improved; you are here to be exposed and then clothed. This week, when something in the sermon convicts you, resist both reactions the dust offers — despair (“I’ll never measure up”) and self-defense (“it’s not that bad”). Instead, let the conviction do its appointed work: “This shows my need. I take it straight to Christ, who met this demand for me.” Train yourself, from week one, to turn exposure into worship.

practices.title: BRING YOUR BANKRUPTCY TO THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to clean yourself up before you come to Jesus. Reverse it. The kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit — to the man who comes empty-handed. This week, practice coming to Christ precisely in your poverty: “Lord, I have no righteousness of my own that could ever surpass the Pharisees. I come as a beggar, and I receive your righteousness as a gift.” When the urge to qualify yourself returns, answer it: I come poor, and the kingdom is given to the poor.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO MAKE YOU HUNGER
practices.body: A man cannot be satisfied with Christ’s righteousness until he hungers for it, and the dust keeps him full on his own. This week, ask the Spirit to do what only he can: “Holy Spirit, expose my self-righteousness and make me hunger and thirst for the righteousness only Christ can give. Empty me, so I can be filled.” Then watch how differently the sermon reads when you are starving for Christ instead of defending yourself.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHERE YOU STAND
practices.body: The dust thrives in isolation and loves to keep a man’s true confidence hidden. Before the week ends, tell one trusted man the honest answer to question one — whose righteousness you have really been trusting — and ask him to remind you, as this study goes on, to keep looking to Christ’s righteousness and not your own. A man sees his self-righteousness most clearly when he says it out loud to a brother.

title: The Mountain and the Righteousness That Surpasses
subtitle: from dust to a borrowed righteousness
keyVerse: For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

passage.text: Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
He opened his mouth and taught them, saying,
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.
Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
“Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
“You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
“Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
For most certainly, I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law, until all things are accomplished.

Whoever, therefore, shall break one of these least commandments, and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE SURPASSING RIGHTEOUSNESS
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Do not rush to the question. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about beginning to obey the sermon better by Friday. It is about learning to read it rightly: as a mirror that drives you to Christ, not a ladder that leaves you in the dust.
prayer: Father, I have no righteousness of my own that could stand before you. I have counted my decency, my churchgoing, my better-than-him. Take it off the books. Lord Jesus, you kept every word of this sermon, and you did it for me. Clothe me in what you earned. Holy Spirit, make me hungry for that righteousness, not full of my own. I come poor today. Let me rise clothed.
prayerLines: Father, I have no righteousness of my own that could stand before you.
I have counted my decency, my churchgoing, my better-than-him.
Take it off the books.
Lord Jesus, you kept every word of this sermon, and you did it for me.
Clothe me in what you earned.
Holy Spirit, make me hungry for that righteousness, not full of my own.
I come poor today. Let me rise clothed.
bottomLine: Matthew 5:20 sets a bar most men spend their whole lives trying to clear and never can: a righteousness that surpasses the most religious men alive. The way into the kingdom is not a better climb. It is a borrowed righteousness — the perfect obedience of Christ, who fulfilled the law you could never keep, credited to the beggar who comes empty-handed. You do not enter by your performance this week. You enter clothed in his, and the rest of this study is learning to live as a man who has stopped trusting his own.
benediction: Brother, before this sermon has demanded a single thing of you, it has already told you the truth that will carry you through all twelve weeks: the righteousness that enters the kingdom is higher than anything you will ever produce. The dust will use that to crush you if it can — whispering that the bar is too high, that you will never measure up, that you may as well stop trying. But the height of the bar is not meant to crush you. It is meant to turn you. It is meant to lift your eyes off your own striving and onto the only One who ever stood on that summit and never once slipped.

So when the sermon exposes you in the weeks to come — and it will, over and over — lift up your eyes. When you see your anger and your lust and your love of money and your anxious unbelieving heart laid bare, lift up your eyes. When the verdict comes that your righteousness falls infinitely short, lift up your eyes to the One whose righteousness does not. Jesus climbed the mountain and preached the law in all its terrifying fullness, and then he went down and lived it — every word, in thought and deed, without a single failure — and walked all the way to a cross to give that flawless righteousness to men who had none. He kept the sermon so that his keeping could be counted as yours.

This is from dust to revival, and it starts by giving up the one thing a religious man clings to hardest: his own righteousness. Not a better performance. Not a cleaner week. A man with his soul clinging to the dust, lifting his eyes off himself, and hearing the Father credit to him the perfect obedience of the Son — a righteousness that surpasses the scribes and Pharisees, because it is the righteousness of God himself. That is your standing. The sermon will spend twelve weeks showing you that you could never earn it, so that you will spend the rest of your life resting in the fact that you do not have to.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of your own failed righteousness. But in Christ you are clothed in a righteousness that surpasses. Lift up your eyes — you enter on his.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop trusting your own righteousness this week, and rest in the righteousness of Christ that surpasses the scribes and Pharisees?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
pulls: Jesus does not bless the man who has arrived. He blesses the man who knows he is empty — and hands him the kingdom.
paras: The dust tells a man that the blessing of God belongs to the impressive. It whispers that God smiles on the strong, the disciplined, the put-together — the men who have their spiritual act in order — and that a man clinging to the floor, weak and weary and full of failure, is the last person heaven would call blessed. So a man hides his poverty. He performs strength he does not have. He tries to clean himself up enough to qualify for a blessing he is sure is reserved for better men.

Then Jesus opens the greatest sermon ever preached, and the first word out of his mouth is blessed — and he aims it at exactly the men the dust has written off. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn. Blessed are the gentle. Blessed are those who hunger. He does not bless the spiritually rich, the self-satisfied, the strong. He pronounces the favor of God over the bankrupt, the grieving, the lowly, and the starving. The kingdom does not open to the man who has it together. It opens to the man who knows he does not.

sections.heading: The Door Is Lower Than You Think
paras: Every man instinctively believes the door into God’s favor is high — that you climb up to it, that you reach it by becoming more. The Beatitudes turn the door upside down. The way in is not up but down: down into honesty about your poverty, down into grief over your sin, down into the gentleness of a man with nothing to defend, down into the hunger of one who knows he has no righteousness of his own. The door into the kingdom is so low that only a man on his knees can pass through it.

This is why the Beatitudes are not a checklist of virtues to achieve before God will bless you. They are a portrait of the man the gospel produces — a man who has stopped pretending, who knows his need, who has come to the end of himself and found the kingdom waiting there. They describe not the qualifications for grace but the marks of a man who has already been gripped by it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Poor in Spirit: The Foundation of Them All
paras: The first beatitude is the door to all the rest: blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. To be poor in spirit is to be spiritually bankrupt and to know it — to stand before God with empty hands, no merit to plead, no righteousness to offer, nothing but need. It is the tax collector beating his chest, unable even to lift his eyes, crying, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. And Jesus says the kingdom belongs to that man, not to the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like other men.

Notice this is not a virtue you work up; it is a truth you wake up to. You do not become poor in spirit by trying to feel humble. You become poor in spirit when the Spirit shows you what you actually are apart from Christ — a beggar, with nothing. And the moment you stop pretending otherwise, the kingdom is handed to you, not as a wage for your humility but as a gift to your empty hands. The dust says your emptiness disqualifies you. Jesus says your emptiness, honestly owned, is the very thing he blesses.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Mourning and Meekness: The Shape of the Blessed Life
paras: The next beatitudes deepen the portrait. Blessed are those who mourn — not merely the grieving in general, but men who grieve their own sin, who feel the weight of what their hearts produce and do not laugh it off. The world tells a man to make peace with his sin, to stop being so hard on himself. Jesus blesses the man who mourns it, because that mourning is the doorway to comfort — the comfort of forgiveness, the comfort of a Savior who carried the very sin you weep over.

Blessed are the gentle — the lowly, the men who have stopped straining to prove and defend themselves. Gentleness is not weakness; it is strength under the hand of God, the posture of a man who no longer has to win every argument or justify himself because his standing is secure in Christ. The dust drives a man to grasp, to defend, to claw for his place. The earth is inherited by the gentle man who has laid all that down, knowing the earth itself is already promised to him in Christ.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Hunger That Will Be Filled
paras: Then comes the beatitude that names what every man in the dust most needs: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.” Jesus does not bless those who possess righteousness; he blesses those who hunger for it — men painfully aware they do not have it, aching for a rightness with God they cannot produce. This is the appetite the dust tries to kill, convincing a man either that he already has enough righteousness or that he never will, so he should stop wanting it.

But Jesus attaches a promise to the hunger: they shall be filled. Filled to the full. The man who hungers for a righteousness he cannot manufacture will be fed — not with his own striving, but with the righteousness of Christ, given freely to the starving. This is the engine of the whole sermon. Every demand it makes is designed to deepen your hunger, and every hunger it deepens, Christ stands ready to satisfy. The blessed man is not the one who is full of himself. He is the one starving for Christ, who gets filled.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Kingdom of the Poor
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the lowest place: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word of the Beatitudes is this: the kingdom is for men exactly like you. Not for the strong who have climbed above the dust, but for the poor who are honest about lying in it. Your poverty of spirit is not the obstacle to blessing; it is the doorway. Your mourning over sin is not a sign you are far from God; it is the path to his comfort. Your hunger for a righteousness you lack is not your disqualification; it is the appetite Christ promises to fill.

So this week, stop trying to qualify for the blessing by becoming impressive. The Beatitudes have already named you blessed in your need, if that need drives you to Christ. Come poor. Come mourning. Come gentle. Come hungry. And receive the kingdom that Jesus gives, not to the rich in themselves, but to the bankrupt who look to him.

stations.verse: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
stations.question: The kingdom belongs to the spiritually bankrupt. Where am I still performing strength instead of admitting my poverty before God?
stations.gloss: blessed, deeply and divinely favored
stations.live: When you feel least blessed — weak, empty, failing — remember whom Jesus calls makarios. The favor of God rests on the poor who come to him, not the strong who don’t need to.
body: Makarios is not a shallow happiness that depends on circumstances; it is the settled state of being favored by God, blessed from a source nothing in the world can touch. Jesus pronounces this deep blessing not over the strong but over the poor in spirit. The favor of God does not rest where the dust says it should — on the impressive — but on the man who knows his need and brings it to Christ.

stations.verse: But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.
stations.question: Two men prayed; the one who admitted he was a sinner went home justified. Which man’s prayer sounds more like mine this week?

stations.verse: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
stations.question: Jesus blesses those who mourn their sin. Have I made peace with sin the world told me to stop grieving — and what would honest mourning look like?
stations.gloss: to mourn, to lament
stations.live: Do not rush past your grief over sin or bury it. Bring it to Christ, who turns the mourning of the forgiven into comfort no one else can give.
body: Pentheō is the word for mourning — lament over loss, including mourning for the dead. Jesus blesses the man who grieves his sin like that, who does not minimize it or laugh it off. James uses the same word when he calls sinners to “lament, mourn, and weep.” And to that mourner Jesus promises comfort: the comfort of a Savior who bore the very sin being wept over. Grief over sin is not the enemy of joy. It is the road to the deepest comfort there is.

stations.verse: Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.
stations.question: Meekness lays down the need to defend and prove myself. Where am I still grasping and clawing for a place that Christ has already secured for me?
stations.gloss: gentle, meek
stations.live: Pick one place this week where you usually push to win — an argument, a slight, a point of pride — and let it go. Your standing is already secured by the gentle One who gave it.
body: Praus is the word Jesus uses of himself: “I am gentle and humble in heart.” So the gentle man is not the man with no strength. He is the man who has stopped needing to win. He does not have to prove himself, defend every inch, or settle every score, because his standing is not up for grabs. And notice what Jesus promises him. Not that he will take the earth. That he will inherit it. An inheritance is not seized. It is given, because of whose son you are.

stations.verse: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.
stations.question: Do I actually hunger for a righteousness I cannot produce — or have I quietly stopped wanting what only Christ can give?
stations.gloss: to hunger, to crave, to be famished
stations.live: Let your sense of lack drive your appetite, not your despair. Bring the hunger to Christ — he has promised to fill the famished, not the full.
body: Peinaō is the gnawing hunger of a man who has not eaten, the craving of genuine need, not a passing preference. Jesus blesses this kind of hunger for righteousness — the deep, aching want of a man who knows he lacks it. The dust either tells you that you are already full or that you will never be fed. Jesus says the famished man who hungers for righteousness will be filled with a righteousness Christ supplies.

stations.verse: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
stations.question: Mercy, purity of heart, peacemaking — these flow from a heart changed by grace. Which one is the Spirit pressing on me this week, and where do I fall short?

stations.verse: For my hand has made all these things, and so all these things came to be,” says Yahweh: “but I will look to this man, even to he who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
stations.question: God says he looks with favor on the humble and contrite. Is my heart soft and trembling before his Word, or hard and self-assured?

stations.verse: You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men. You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
stations.question: Salt and light flow from a heart already blessed, not from striving. Is my life pointing others to the Father, or to myself?
stations.gloss: light, that which makes things visible
stations.live: You do not generate the light; you reflect it. Let your life this week point past you to the Father, the true source of every good thing in you.
body: Phōs is light — not light a man manufactures, but light that shines because it has a source. Jesus does not command you to become light by effort; he declares you are light, and tells you to let it shine. The blessed man, made new by grace, shines not to display himself but so that others see the Father. The light is borrowed, and its whole purpose is to point beyond the one carrying it.

stations.verse: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
stations.question: God opposes pride but pours grace on the humble. Where is pride still costing me grace I could be receiving?
pulls: The door into the kingdom is so low that only a man on his knees can pass through it.

practices.title: STOP PERFORMING STRENGTH YOU DON’T HAVE
practices.body: Most men carry a performance — a projected strength that hides the poverty underneath. This week, name yours. Where are you pretending to have it together before God and other men? Write it down, then write across it the truth of Matthew 5:3: blessed are the poor in spirit. You do not have to perform your way into blessing. The kingdom is given to the man who drops the act and admits he is empty.

practices.title: LET YOURSELF MOURN, THEN TAKE IT TO COMFORT
practices.body: The world tells you to stop being hard on yourself; Jesus blesses the man who mourns his sin. This week, when you sin, do not minimize it and do not wallow in it — mourn it honestly, and then carry that mourning straight to Christ for comfort. Pray it: “Lord, I grieve this, and I bring the grief to you, the One who bore it. Comfort me with your forgiveness.” Godly mourning that ends at the cross becomes the deepest comfort there is.

practices.title: BRING YOUR HUNGER TO THE SON
practices.body: You will be tempted to either feel full of your own righteousness or despair of ever having any. Reverse both. Bring your hunger to Jesus, who promised to fill it. This week, when you feel your lack of righteousness, turn it into appetite: “Lord, I hunger for a righteousness I cannot produce. Satisfy me with yours.” The man who hungers for Christ’s righteousness will be filled — he said so.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO KEEP YOU POOR IN SPIRIT
practices.body: Poverty of spirit is not natural; the dust constantly inflates a man back into self-sufficiency. This week, ask the Spirit to keep showing you your need: “Holy Spirit, keep me poor in spirit. Show me my true poverty apart from Christ, so I keep coming to him with empty hands.” Then receive the kingdom he gives to the empty, again and again.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHAT YOU’RE HIDING
practices.body: The performance of strength is reinforced in isolation and broken in honest company. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother one place you have been pretending to be stronger than you are, and let him remind you that the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit. A man stops performing when he finds he is still loved after he admits he is empty.

title: Blessed Are the Bankrupt
subtitle: from dust to the kingdom of the poor
keyVerse: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

passage.text: Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
He opened his mouth and taught them, saying,
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.
Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
“Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
“You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp, and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE BLESSING OF THE EMPTY
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about manufacturing humility by Friday. It is about waking up to the truth that the kingdom is given to the poor, and coming to Christ as the empty man you are.
prayer: Father, I am poorer than I let on. I have hidden the need, dressed up the weakness, and called it strength. I bring it to you now, empty-handed. Lord Jesus, you bless the poor in spirit and fill the hungry. Fill me, because I have nothing to bring. Holy Spirit, keep me honest about my sin, and let me mourn it in a way that runs to comfort. Give me the gentleness of a man who no longer has to win.
prayerLines: Father, I am poorer than I let on.
I have hidden the need, dressed up the weakness, and called it strength.
I bring it to you now, empty-handed.
Lord Jesus, you bless the poor in spirit and fill the hungry.
Fill me, because I have nothing to bring.
Holy Spirit, keep me honest about my sin, and let me mourn it in a way that runs to comfort.
Give me the gentleness of a man who no longer has to win.
bottomLine: The Beatitudes open the greatest sermon ever preached by blessing exactly the men the dust writes off — the poor in spirit, the mourning, the gentle, the hungry. The kingdom is not a wage paid to the impressive; it is a gift handed to the bankrupt who come to Christ with empty hands. You do not qualify for the blessing by becoming strong. You receive it by admitting you are poor, mourning your sin, and hungering for a righteousness only Christ can give — and being filled.
benediction: Brother, the dust has told you for years that God’s blessing is reserved for better men — stronger men, more disciplined men, men who do not cling to the floor the way you do. Lift your eyes off that lie and onto the first words of the greatest sermon ever preached. When Jesus opened his mouth to teach, he did not bless the impressive. He blessed the poor in spirit, the mourning, the gentle, the hungry. He pronounced the favor of God over exactly the kind of man the dust had convinced was beyond it. The kingdom of heaven, he said, belongs to the bankrupt who know they are bankrupt and come to him.

So when you feel too poor, too weak, too full of failure to be blessed, lift up your eyes. When you mourn your sin and the dust says God is disgusted with you, lift up your eyes — he blesses the mourner and promises him comfort. When you hunger for a righteousness you know you do not have, lift up your eyes — he blesses the hungry and promises to fill them. Jesus took on flesh and became poor for your sake, was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, hungered and thirsted in a wilderness for you, so that he could fill your poverty with his riches and your hunger with his righteousness.

This is from dust to revival — not a man climbing out of his poverty to earn a blessing, but a man discovering that Jesus blesses him in his poverty and hands him the kingdom. You do not have to become someone else to be favored by God. You have to come as you are, poor and mourning and hungry, to the King who blesses the empty and fills the starving. Lift up your eyes to the One who calls you blessed, and receive the kingdom that belongs to the poor.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust and feels too poor to be blessed. But the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit. Lift up your eyes — he calls you blessed.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop performing strength this week, and come to Christ as the poor, mourning, hungry man the Beatitudes already call blessed?

sections.heading: The Comfort of a Lowered Law
pulls: You thought you had kept this commandment because your hands are clean. Jesus reads your heart — and there has been murder there all along.
paras: There is a particular comfort a man takes in a law he can keep. Have you murdered anyone? No. Good — then on that commandment, at least, the ledger is clean. This is exactly how the scribes and Pharisees handled the law: they drew its boundaries narrowly enough that they could stay safely inside, and then rested in their record. As long as the hand had not done the deed, the man considered himself innocent. It is a comfort built on a lie, but it is a comfort, and men cling to it.

Then Jesus takes that comfort apart. “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’” but Jesus says “that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment.” The man who holds his brother in contempt — who calls him Raca, who calls him a fool, who writes him off as worthless — is “in danger of the fire of Gehenna.” Jesus drives the commandment off the surface and down into the heart, and in one stroke he turns a law most men think they have kept into a law every man has shattered. The murderer and the man nursing contempt stand, in the court of the heart, on the same ground.

sections.heading: The Law Was Always About the Heart
paras: Jesus is not adding a stricter rule to an old one. He is revealing what the commandment always meant. God never gave the sixth commandment merely to keep hands off throats; he gave it to expose and forbid the hatred in the heart from which murder grows. Cain’s hand killed Abel, but the murder began in Cain’s furious, contemptuous heart long before. The law against murder was always a law against the anger and contempt that despise the image of God in another man.

This is why the Sermon on the Mount is such a mirror. The Pharisee read the law and saw a standard he had met. Jesus reads the same law and shows you a heart full of resentment, dismissal, simmering grudges, and quiet contempt for the people who have wronged you — and tells you that this, too, is what the commandment forbids. The man who thought he was a law-keeper discovers he is a heart-murderer, and the comfort of the lowered law collapses.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Anger and Contempt Are the Murder God Sees
paras: Look closely at what Jesus indicts. Not only the white-hot rage that wants someone dead, but the everyday anger a man nurses against his brother without a cause. Every angry man is sure he has one. That is the trap. Held up to Christ, most of your anger turns out to be pride wounded, not righteousness offended. And Jesus names the contempt packed into a word like Raca — you empty-headed fool, you nothing. Jesus says the man who harbors that anger is in danger of the judgment, and the man who pours out that contempt is in danger of the fire. He is naming the precise sins respectable men commit every day and excuse instantly: the grudge, the dismissal, the silent writing-off of another human being.

Be honest about how thoroughly this exposes you. The driver who cut you off, the coworker who undermined you, the family member who wounded you years ago — the contempt you feel toward them, the way you have reduced them in your heart to less than human, is what Jesus here calls murder’s kin. You may never lift a hand. But God does not grade on the hand. He sees the heart, and in the heart, the verdict is guilty.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Reconciliation Matters More Than Religion
paras: Then Jesus presses it into the most religious moment imaginable. “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” He will not let a man paper over a fractured relationship with religious activity. The contempt in your heart is not canceled by the offering in your hand. God wants the heart set right with your brother more than he wants your gift.

This is devastating to the religious man who uses worship to avoid repentance, who keeps coming to the altar while keeping his grudges intact. Jesus says the two cannot coexist. The man who will not be reconciled to his brother has not understood the gospel that reconciled him to God. And here the mirror does its deepest work: you cannot, by willpower, manufacture a heart free of anger and contempt. You can try to behave — but the resentment remains, and God sees it. You need more than better behavior. You need a new heart.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The One Who Was Called a Fool in Your Place
paras: This is where the weight becomes good news. If anger and contempt put a man in danger of the judgment, then you stand condemned — and that is exactly the point that drives you to Christ. For there was one man who never once nursed anger in his heart, never held a single soul in contempt, never reduced a person to less than the image of God. Jesus loved perfectly, even his enemies, even those who drove the nails. He kept the sixth commandment all the way down to the bottom of his heart, where no other man ever has.

And then this perfectly loving man was treated as the heart-murderer. He was mocked, spat on, called every contemptuous name, declared worthless, and condemned to the death of a criminal — he, the only man who was ever truly innocent in heart. He took the judgment your anger deserves. He absorbed the contempt that should fall on you. And in exchange, his perfect, loving heart is credited to you, and his Spirit goes to work cleansing the very anger and contempt the law exposed. The mirror showed you a murderer’s heart; the cross gives you a new one.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Heart Christ Cleanses
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man whose heart has just been exposed as a nest of anger and contempt is this: there is one whose heart was clean, and he died for yours. You are not left to scrub the resentment out by sheer effort, which never works anyway. You are pointed to the Christ who kept this commandment perfectly, bore your guilt for breaking it, and now sends his Spirit to make your heart like his.

So this week, when the law exposes the anger you have excused and the contempt you have hidden, do not despair and do not minimize. Let the exposure drive you to the cross. Confess the murder in your heart, receive the forgiveness purchased by the One condemned in your place, and ask the Spirit to begin cleansing what willpower never could. The man who sees his anger rightly and runs to Christ is being revived — from the dust of a guilty heart to a heart Christ is making new.

stations.verse: You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’ But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
stations.question: Jesus says my anger and contempt put me in danger of the judgment. Whose face comes to mind when I read this — and what does that reveal about my heart?
stations.gloss: empty-head, worthless one — a word of contempt
stations.live: Notice the contempt you pass off as honesty — the people you have written off in your heart. Name it as the sin Jesus says it is, and bring it to the cross.
body: Raca is an Aramaic word carried over into the Greek text — most likely from a word meaning “empty.” It was a word of withering contempt, calling a man brainless and worthless, reducing a human being made in God’s image to nothing. Jesus puts this everyday insult in the same indictment as murder, because both spring from a heart that despises another person. The sin is not only in the fist. It is in the verdict the heart passes on a brother.

stations.verse: Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
stations.question: John says hatred is murder. Is there a grudge I have been carrying that God calls by a far more serious name than I do?
stations.gloss: a murderer, a manslayer
stations.live: When you catch yourself nursing hatred this week, call it by John’s word. Then set it beside the One who laid down his life for you.
body: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. John uses it for the man who hates his brother. Jesus uses it for the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning.” That is the company hatred keeps. It is a blunt word, and John means it bluntly. But the next verse gives the answer: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us.” The murderer takes a life. Christ laid his down — for men who had hated.

stations.verse: If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
stations.question: God wants me reconciled more than he wants my worship. Is there a relationship I am avoiding while still going through religious motions?
stations.gloss: to change enmity for friendship, to be reconciled
stations.live: Name the man who has something against you. Before Sunday, go — a call, a visit, a plain word. Leave the offering and settle it.
body: This is the only place the word appears in the New Testament. It means to trade hostility for friendship, and the lexicon notes it carries the sense of concession on both sides after hostility on both sides. Jesus does not tell you to wait until your brother comes to you. He tells you to leave the gift on the altar and go. The one who knows he has been reconciled to God is the one who can walk across the room first.

stations.verse: Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.
stations.question: God warned Cain about anger before it became murder. Where is anger crouching at my door right now, unaddressed?
stations.gloss: to be angry, to nurse settled, simmering anger
stations.live: Do not feed the smolder. When anger settles in and starts to nurse itself, take it to Christ before it grows — confess it as sin, not as a grievance you are owed.
body: Orgizomai describes not a flash of emotion but a settled, smoldering anger — the kind a man nurses and feeds over time. This is the anger Jesus places under judgment: not the momentary reaction, but the resentment harbored and held. It is the anger that crouched at Cain’s door and grew into murder. God sees the smoldering long before it becomes a flame, and he calls the smoldering itself sin.

stations.verse: Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.
stations.question: I am to forgive as God forgave me in Christ. Where am I withholding from another the very mercy I have received?

stations.verse: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
stations.question: My anger does not produce God’s righteousness, though I often act as if it does. Where am I justifying anger as if it were holy?

stations.verse: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
stations.question: David asked God to create a clean heart, knowing he could not produce one himself. Am I trying to clean my own heart, or asking God to make it new?
stations.gloss: to create, to shape, to form
stations.live: Stop trying to scrub your own heart clean of anger and contempt. Ask God to create what you cannot — a clean heart — and trust the Spirit to do the making.
body: This is the verb of Genesis 1:1: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.” In its main stem it always has God as its subject. Men build, make, and mend. Only God bārāʾ. So David does not ask God to repair his heart or help him try harder. He uses the one verb that belongs to God alone: create in me a clean heart. A clean heart is beyond human manufacture. It is a creative act of God, not a self-improvement project of man.

stations.verse: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
stations.question: God promises to replace the heart of stone, not merely improve it. Do I believe he can soften the hardness I have given up on?

stations.verse: When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
stations.question: Jesus absorbed contempt without returning it, keeping the very commandment I break. How does his perfect heart, credited to me, change how I face those who wrong me?
pulls: The mirror showed you a murderer’s heart. The cross gives you a new one.

practices.title: NAME THE CONTEMPT YOU CALL HONESTY
practices.body: Most men carry contempt they have rebranded as discernment — people they have written off, reduced, dismissed in their hearts, all while feeling justified. This week, name yours. Whose face came to mind when you read “You fool”? Write the name down, then write across it the truth from Matthew 5: this anger, this contempt, is what Jesus says puts a man in danger of the judgment. You cannot bring to the cross a sin you keep calling something else.

practices.title: LET THE EXPOSURE DRIVE YOU TO THE CROSS, NOT TO DESPAIR
practices.body: When Jesus shows you the murder in your heart, the dust offers two exits: despair (“I’m a hateful man, beyond help”) or minimizing (“It’s just righteous anger”). Refuse both. This week, when anger or contempt surfaces, take it straight to Christ: “Lord, this is the sin you died for. I bring it to the One condemned in my place.” Let conviction become confession, and confession become worship of the Savior who bore it.

practices.title: BE RECONCILED BEFORE YOU WORSHIP
practices.body: Jesus says to leave your gift at the altar and go be reconciled first. This week, identify one fractured relationship you have been avoiding while still going through religious motions. Take a real step — a conversation, a confession, an apology, a reaching out. Pray it through Christ: “Lord, you reconciled me to God while I was your enemy. Give me the grace to take the first step toward my brother.” Do not let worship become a way of avoiding repentance.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT FOR A CLEAN HEART
practices.body: You cannot scrub anger out of your own heart; David knew a clean heart must be created, not manufactured. This week, pray Psalm 51 daily: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Remove the contempt I cannot remove. Make my heart like Christ’s.” Then cooperate with the Spirit’s cleansing instead of merely managing your behavior. The goal is not a man who hides his anger better, but a heart being made new.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER THE GRUDGE YOU’RE HOLDING
practices.body: Anger and contempt grow in the dark, nursed in private and justified in silence. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother about a grudge you have been carrying, and ask him to help you bring it to Christ rather than feed it. Spoken aloud to a brother, a grudge often shrinks to the size it really is — a sin to be confessed, not a right to be defended.

title: The Heart Behind the Hand
subtitle: from dust to the heart Christ cleanses
keyVerse: You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’ But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.

passage.text: “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there, until you have paid the last penny.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE HEART BEHIND THE HAND
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about white-knuckling your anger into submission by Friday. It is about letting Christ’s words expose the heart behind your hands, taking the guilt to the cross, and asking the Spirit to cleanse what you cannot.
prayer: Father, there is anger in me I have called justice. There are names I have written off in my heart. I confess it as the murder Jesus says it is. Lord Jesus, you were called worthless and condemned in my place, and you never once held contempt. Take my guilty heart to your cross. Holy Spirit, create in me a clean heart. Show me the brother I need to go to, and give me the legs to go.
prayerLines: Father, there is anger in me I have called justice.
There are names I have written off in my heart.
I confess it as the murder Jesus says it is.
Lord Jesus, you were called worthless and condemned in my place, and you never once held contempt.
Take my guilty heart to your cross.
Holy Spirit, create in me a clean heart.
Show me the brother I need to go to, and give me the legs to go.
bottomLine: Matthew 5:21–22 takes a commandment most men think they have kept and drives it into the heart, where anger and contempt stand condemned alongside murder. The comfort of the lowered law collapses, and every man is exposed as guilty. But there was one man whose heart never held contempt — who loved perfectly, was condemned as a murderer in your place, and now credits his clean heart to you and sends his Spirit to make yours like his. The way out is not to manage your anger better. It is to take your exposed heart to the cross and ask God to create the clean heart you cannot.
benediction: Brother, you have spent years taking quiet comfort in the commandments you thought you kept, and “do not murder” was surely one of them. Your hands are clean of blood. But Jesus has just held up the mirror and shown you what God always saw — the anger you nurse, the contempt you pour out, the brothers you have written off and reduced to nothing in your heart. In the court of heaven, that heart is guilty, and no amount of clean-handed respectability changes the verdict. If the sermon stops there, it crushes you. It is not meant to stop there.

So when the law exposes the murder in your heart this week, lift up your eyes. When you see the grudges and the contempt you have excused for years, lift up your eyes. When the verdict comes back guilty and the dust says you are a hateful man beyond repair, lift up your eyes to the One man who was not. Jesus never once held a soul in contempt. He loved his enemies, prayed for those who killed him, and kept the sixth commandment all the way to the bottom of his heart — and then he, the only innocent heart that ever beat, was mocked and reviled and condemned as a criminal in your place. He was called a fool so that you could be called a son.

This is from dust to revival — not a man scrubbing the anger out of his own heart by willpower, but a man taking his exposed and guilty heart to the cross and receiving a clean one in return. Christ kept the commandment you broke, bore the judgment you deserved, and now sends his Spirit to cleanse the very contempt the law uncovered. You are not left to manage a murderous heart on your own. You are given a new one. Lift up your eyes to the One condemned in your place, and let him make your heart like his.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of a heart full of anger you cannot cleanse. But Christ kept the law and was condemned for you. Lift up your eyes — he gives a clean heart.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop excusing the anger and contempt in your heart this week, and bring it to the Christ who was condemned in your place and gives a clean heart?

sections.heading: Another Commandment a Man Thought He Kept
pulls: The act was never the whole of the sin. Adultery begins in the look, the entertained desire, the heart that takes what is not its own.
paras: Just as he did with murder, Jesus takes a commandment most respectable men believe they have kept and drives it down into the heart, where it shatters every man who hears it honestly. You have heard it said, “Do not commit adultery,” and a married man who has been physically faithful may feel he is on safe ground. Then Jesus closes that ground in a single sentence: “everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” The act was never the whole of the sin. The sin begins in the look, the entertained desire, the heart that takes what is not his to take.

This is not Jesus being harsh; it is Jesus being honest about what the seventh commandment always meant. God never gave it merely to govern bodies. He gave it to govern hearts — to forbid not only the deed of adultery but the inner unfaithfulness, the coveting, the using of another person in the imagination for one’s own pleasure. And by that standard, no honest man stands acquitted. The mirror of the sermon shows a man that his eyes and his imagination have made him an adulterer many times over, even if his body never moved from where it stood.

sections.heading: Why This Conviction Is Mercy, Not Cruelty
paras: A man may feel that Jesus is simply piling on guilt here, naming a sin so universal and so deeply rooted that no one could ever be free of it. But the severity is mercy. If lust were only a behavior, a man might manage it by sheer willpower and live with a quiet pride in his control. By exposing it as a matter of the heart, Jesus strips away that false comfort and shows a man his real condition: he does not merely do unclean things; he is, in his heart, unclean. And a man who sees that he needs cleansing, not just better behavior, is finally in a position to look to the only One who can give it.

So the conviction of this week is not meant to bury you. It is meant to drive you off the project of self-managed purity, which always fails in the end, and onto the Christ who was pure in heart in your place and gives his purity to you. The sermon shows you a heart you cannot clean. The gospel offers you a heart Christ will make new. Conviction here, as everywhere in this sermon, is the road to grace, not the dead end of despair.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Lust Is the Heart Taking What Is Not Its Own
paras: Look carefully at what Jesus indicts. Not the involuntary first glance, not the temptation that arrives unbidden, but the gaze to lust after her — the look that lingers on purpose, the desire welcomed and fed, the imagination that undresses and uses another person made in God’s image. This is coveting turned toward a human being: the heart reaching out to seize what God has not given it, treating a person as an object for private consumption. The sin is not that desire exists; it is that the heart entertains and feeds a desire for what is not its own to take.

Be honest about how thoroughly this exposes a man in an age built to inflame it. The screen, the scroll, the second look, the fantasy nursed in private — all of it is the heart taking what is not its own, and all of it Jesus names as adultery of the heart. A man may have constructed an entire secret life of the imagination while believing himself faithful because his body stayed home. The Word will not allow that self-deception. It calls the lingering look what God calls it, and it leaves the respectable man exposed alongside the obvious sinner.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Violence of the Cure
paras: Then Jesus says something startling: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you.” “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you.” He is not commanding self-mutilation — a blind man can still lust. He is using deliberate, shocking language to convey how deadly this sin is and how violently it must be fought. A man who is casual about lust has not understood what is at stake. Jesus says it would be better to lose an eye or a hand than to let sin drag the whole self into destruction. The cure is not gentle management; it is radical, ruthless severance from whatever feeds the sin.

This is a word every man tempted this way needs to hear, because the dust loves to negotiate with lust, to keep one channel open, to handle it gently. Jesus says handle it like the deadly thing it is. Whatever the eye and the hand are reaching for that feeds the sin — cut it off, throw it away, take the loss. But even this radical severance is not the source of a clean heart. It is the necessary cutting a forgiven man does, but the cleansing itself comes from somewhere the knife cannot reach. A man can amputate every occasion of sin and still have a lustful heart. He needs more than amputation. He needs a Savior.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Weight of the Word on Marriage
paras: Jesus moves from lust to marriage, and he speaks with sobering weight about the covenant of marriage and the seriousness of breaking it. He refuses the casual, self-serving approach to divorce that the men of his day had constructed to suit themselves, and he restores marriage to the high and holy thing God made it — a covenant not to be discarded for convenience. Here again the Word exposes a man’s heart: the ways he has treated his own covenant lightly, failed to cherish and protect it, let his heart wander from the wife of his youth in a thousand small unfaithfulnesses long before any larger one.

And here, too, the gospel speaks. For the man who hears these words and feels the weight of his failures in marriage — his hardness, his selfishness, his wandering heart, his covenant kept poorly or broken outright — there is a Bridegroom who has kept his covenant perfectly. Christ loves his bride, the church, with a faithfulness no human husband has ever matched, and he gave himself up for her to make her clean. The man who has failed his covenant is not left only with his failure; he is pointed to the faithful Bridegroom whose perfect covenant-love covers the unfaithful and teaches them, slowly, to love as he loves.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to a Clean Heart
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man whose eyes and imagination and covenant failures have just been laid bare is this: there was one man who was pure in heart, who never once took with his eyes what was not his, who kept covenant perfectly — and he gives his purity to the impure. Jesus was “in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” He looked on no one with lust, used no one in his heart, and his flawless purity is credited to men whose hearts are anything but pure.

So this week, when the sermon exposes the adultery of your eyes and the failures of your covenant, do not despair and do not minimize. The cutting is real — cut off what feeds the sin, as Jesus commands — but the cleansing comes from the cross, not the knife. Confess the impurity, receive the forgiveness Christ purchased, and ask the Spirit to create in you the clean heart you cannot create yourself. The man who sees his heart’s adultery and runs to Christ is being revived, from the dust of a heart he cannot clean to a purity that is given, and a heart the Spirit is making new.

stations.verse: You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery;’ but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.
stations.question: Jesus says lust is adultery of the heart. Where have I told myself I am faithful because my body stayed home, while my eyes and imagination wandered?
stations.gloss: to covet, to crave, to set the heart on having
stations.live: Learn the difference between the temptation that arrives and the desire you feed. Refuse the second look and the welcomed craving — and take even the involuntary pull to Christ.
body: Epithymeō is the word for coveting — the same desire forbidden in the tenth commandment, now turned toward a person. It is not the temptation that arrives unbidden but the heart’s reaching to seize what is not given, to have and use what belongs to another or to God alone. Jesus exposes lust as coveting aimed at a human being made in God’s image. The sin is not that desire exists; it is the heart welcoming and feeding the craving to take what is not its own.

stations.verse: I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?
stations.question: Job made a covenant with his eyes. What would it look like for me to make a deliberate, specific covenant with mine this week?
stations.gloss: covenant, a binding pledge
stations.live: Make a specific covenant with your eyes this week — name the screen, the hour, the place. Then pray it in the strength of the new covenant, not your own.
body: Bərît is the word for the great binding promises of God — the covenant he made with Abram, the new covenant he promised through Jeremiah. Job borrows it for a promise about where his eyes will go. That is good sense, and you should make that covenant too. But mark the difference. Job’s covenant depends on Job. The new covenant depends on God: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart.” Your eyes keep a covenant best when your heart has been rewritten.

stations.verse: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna. If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna.
stations.question: Jesus commands a radical cutting-off of whatever feeds this sin. What specifically do I need to cut off or throw away — and what loss am I refusing to take?
stations.gloss: to put a snare in the way; to cause to stumble
stations.live: Identify the specific trigger that springs the trap for you — the app, the route, the screen, the situation — and cut it off ruthlessly. Take the loss; it is cheaper than the snare.
body: Skandalizō comes from skandalon, a snare or stumbling-block laid in the path. The lexicon gives its first sense plainly: to put a snare or stumbling-block in the way. Jesus uses it for whatever in your life trips you into sin: the eye, the hand, the thing they reach for. His command is ruthless — remove it, cut it off, take the loss — because the alternative is to be caught. A man casual about what trips him has not seen the snare for what it is.

stations.verse: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
stations.question: Jesus blesses the pure in heart — a purity I do not possess. Am I trying to manufacture it, or asking Christ to give me his?

stations.verse: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.
stations.question: David asked God to create a clean heart, knowing he could not produce one. Am I still trying to clean my own, or asking God to make it new?
stations.gloss: clean, pure, free from contamination
stations.live: Stop trying to scrub your own heart clean. Ask God to create the purity you cannot, and trust the blood of Christ and the Spirit to do what your effort never could.
body: Katharos means clean — unmixed, uncontaminated, pure all the way through. It is the word behind the blessing on the pure in heart and the cry of David for a clean heart. A man cannot make himself katharos by scrubbing harder; the contamination goes deeper than effort can reach. This is why David asks God to create what only God can make. The clean heart is a gift of grace, washed by the blood of Christ and renewed by the Spirit, never the achievement of a man’s willpower.

stations.verse: Some of you were such, but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.
stations.question: Paul says “Some of you were such” — past tense, washed clean. Do I live as a man already washed, or as a man still defined by what he was?

stations.verse: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it; that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word, that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect.
stations.question: Christ loved his bride with a faithfulness I have never matched. Where has my covenant love failed, and how does his perfect love cover and instruct mine?

stations.verse: For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.
stations.question: Jesus was tempted as I am, yet never sinned. How does it change my struggle to know my Savior faced this temptation and never fell — and credits his purity to me?
stations.gloss: to have a fellow feeling with, to sympathize
stations.live: Bring the temptation to Christ while it is live, not after you have lost. He knows the pull, and he never broke.
body: This is the verb behind “touched with the feeling of our infirmities.” Your High Priest is not reading about your temptation from a safe distance. He felt its pull. He “has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.” The same word is used for believers who had compassion on a brother in chains. Christ stands next to you in it — and he never gave way. That means he can help you, and his clean record can cover you.

stations.verse: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
stations.question: There is a specific impurity I am tempted to hide rather than confess. What would it mean to bring even that into the light and receive cleansing?
pulls: The sermon shows you a heart you cannot clean. The gospel o’ers you a heart Christ will make new.

practices.title: NAME THE SELF-DECEPTION
practices.body: Most men tempted this way maintain a quiet self-deception — “I’m faithful because I’ve never actually done it,” while the eyes and imagination roam freely. This week, name yours honestly. Where have you called yourself pure while feeding adultery of the heart? Write it down, then write across it the truth of Matthew 5:28. You cannot bring to Christ a sin you keep excusing. Call it what he calls it, and the door to cleansing opens.

practices.title: MAKE A COVENANT WITH YOUR EYES
practices.body: Job made a covenant with his eyes; vague intentions never beat this sin. This week, make a specific, concrete covenant: name the second look you will refuse, the scroll you will not open, the route you will not take. Write it down as an actual commitment before God. Then, knowing you will not keep it perfectly, pair it with the gospel: “When I fail, I run to Christ for cleansing, not away from him in shame.”

practices.title: CUT O* THE TRIGGER — RUTHLESSLY
