stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE AUDIENCE OF ONE
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about purifying your motives by Friday — a thing no man can do by effort. It is about letting Christ’s words expose the audience you perform for, taking that rotten craving to the cross, and learning to live before the Father who sees in secret.
prayer: Father, I have performed for the wrong audience. I have prayed to be heard by men and given to be seen. You see in secret. Let that be enough. Lord Jesus, you lived your whole life before your Father’s eyes, and your unperformed righteousness is mine. Holy Spirit, teach me to pray short and plain, as a son who already has his Father’s ear.
prayerLines: Father, I have performed for the wrong audience.
I have prayed to be heard by men and given to be seen.
You see in secret. Let that be enough.
Lord Jesus, you lived your whole life before your Father’s eyes,
and your unperformed righteousness is mine.
Holy Spirit, teach me to pray short and plain,
as a son who already has his Father’s ear.
bottomLine: Matthew 6:1–18 turns the mirror of the sermon onto the most hidden room in a man’s heart — his motives — and exposes how thoroughly the craving to be seen corrupts even his giving, his praying, and his fasting. Three times the verdict falls on the performer: he has received his reward, paid in full by the applause he chased, with nothing left from the Father. But there was one man who never once performed for the crowd, who lived his entire life before an audience of One and earned the Father’s “well done” you never could. His secret, unperformed righteousness is credited to you, and his Father becomes your Father. The way out of the exhausting stage is not better motives. It is to rest in the approval Christ already won, and to live, one ordinary day at a time, before the Father who sees in secret.
benediction: Brother, the dust has kept you on a stage for years, performing a righteousness for an audience that can never finally satisfy you — giving so you would be noticed, praying so you would be heard, letting your devotion show so the right people would admire it. And Jesus has just held up the mirror to the most hidden room of your heart and shown you the second audience you keep glancing toward, the craving for human approval that has quietly corrupted even your best deeds. It is exhausting to live on that stage, and it pays only in applause that fades by morning. Lift your eyes off the watching crowd.

When you catch yourself performing this week, lift up your eyes. When you do a quiet good and no one notices and the old hunger for credit rises, lift up your eyes. When you realize how much of your religion has been theater played for people, lift up your eyes to the One man who never once stepped onto that stage. Jesus gave with no trumpet, withdrew alone into the dark to pray where no crowd could see, fasted in a wilderness with no audience but his Father. He lived his whole life before an audience of One, sought no reward but the Father’s pleasure — and then he was stripped naked and lifted up on a cross before a jeering, watching crowd, shamed publicly so that you could be approved secretly. He bore your performing so that you could rest in his pleasing.

This is from dust to revival — not a man straining to purify his own motives, but a man who has stopped performing because he finally believes the Father already sees him and already loves him in Christ. The “well done” you have been chasing from people, Jesus already earned from the Father in your place, and the Father has already spoken it over you: you are my beloved son. You can step off the stage. You can give and pray and fast in secret, not to earn a verdict, but because the verdict is already in. Lift up your eyes to the Father who sees in secret, and live, free at last, for an audience of One.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of the stage, performing for a crowd that never satis-es. But the Father sees you in secret, and in Christ he is pleased. Lift up your eyes — you have an audience of One.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to step off the stage this week, and live your giving, praying, and fasting before the Father who sees in secret — resting in the approval Christ has already won for you?

sections.heading: The Sin That Dresses as Prudence
pulls: The love of money is the one idol a man can serve openly and still be admired. That is exactly why it is so dangerous.
paras: Of all the sins the Sermon on the Mount exposes, this one hides best, because it dresses up as wisdom. No one praises a man for his anger or his lust, but a man can build his whole life around money and be admired for it — prudent, responsible, a good provider, a success. The love of money is the one idol a man can serve openly and still be respected. And that is exactly why it is so dangerous, and why Jesus speaks to it so directly. The danger is not in having money; it is in the heart that quietly bows to it while calling the worship by safer names.

Jesus does not soften it. You cannot serve God and money. He uses the language of slavery — a man is owned by one master or the other, and the heart cannot be split between them. Either God is your treasure and money is your servant, or money is your treasure and God becomes, at best, a means to it. There is no neutral ground, no comfortable middle where a man treasures both. The Word forces the question every man would rather avoid: which one actually owns you?

sections.heading: Your Treasure Reveals Your Heart
paras: Jesus gives a piercing diagnostic: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. He does not say put your heart in the right place and your treasure will follow; he says the reverse. Your treasure leads, and your heart follows it. So if a man wants to know what he actually worships — not what he claims to worship — he need only follow his treasure. Where does his money go without a struggle? What does he daydream about? What loss would devastate him? What, if he is honest, does he most deeply trust to make him secure and happy? The answer is his real god, whatever his lips confess.

This is where the mirror does its work. Most men assume their hearts are fixed on God and would be offended to hear otherwise. But follow the treasure. The anxious checking of the account, the quiet pride in what is owned, the way the mood rises and falls with the markets, the daydreams of more — these are the needle of a compass, and they point at the true treasure. The Word will not let a man rest in what he says he loves. It sends him to follow the trail of his treasure and discover where his heart has actually gone.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Treasure That Cannot Last
paras: Jesus begins with the futility of earthly treasure: do not lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal. Every earthly treasure shares the same fatal flaw — it does not last. The moth eats the fine garment, the rust corrodes the stored metal, the thief carries off the hoard. And beyond all of those, death finally strips a man of everything he has gathered; he carries nothing out of the world. To build your life on earthly treasure is to build it on what is certainly, inevitably, passing away in your hands even as you grip it.

This is not Jesus despising the physical world; it is Jesus being realistic about it. He is the truest economist there is, urging a man not to pour his one life into an investment guaranteed to fail. Lay up treasure in heaven, he says, where nothing decays and no thief can reach — treasure that survives death, treasure kept by God himself. The tragedy of the man with earthly treasure is not that he wanted too much, but that he settled for far too little, hoarding what rots while ignoring what lasts forever.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Eye, the Lamp, and the Whole Body
paras: Then Jesus gives a strange and searching image: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness.” Scripture already used the evil eye for a closed hand: the law warns a man not to let his “eye be evil against your poor brother” and give him nothing (Deuteronomy 15:9), and Proverbs speaks of “him who has a stingy eye.” The sound eye is the single, open-handed one. Jesus is saying that how a man looks at his possessions floods his whole life with either light or darkness. A grasping, greedy eye darkens everything; a generous, open-handed eye fills the whole man with light.

This exposes how total money’s grip can be. It is never just about the bank account; the disposition of the heart toward wealth colors the entire man. A greedy eye warps a man’s relationships, his peace, his worship, his rest — the darkness fills the whole body. And a man cannot simply decide to have a sound eye; greed reaches deeper than resolve. He needs his sight changed, his heart reset on a treasure worthy of it. He needs to be given new eyes that see Christ as more valuable than gold.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: No One Can Serve Two Masters
paras: Jesus drives to the verdict: no one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. Notice he personifies money as a rival master, almost a rival god — because that is what it becomes. Money makes a wonderful servant and a terrible master, and the human heart is forever trying to give it the throne while keeping God on retainer. Jesus says it cannot be done. The throne holds one master, and the heart will serve whichever one sits there.

And here the mirror leaves a man fully exposed, because every honest man knows how often money has been on the throne of his heart. The anxiety, the grasping, the security sought in a number, the willingness to compromise for gain — these are the marks of a heart that has served the wrong master. No amount of trying to serve both will resolve it. A man cannot pry money off the throne by willpower; the heart simply re-enthrones it. What he needs is a treasure so much greater that money is dethroned by something better — and that treasure is Christ himself.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to Treasure That Lasts
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man whose heart has been exposed as divided, serving money while claiming to serve God, is this: there is a treasure that does not rot, and it was bought for you at infinite cost. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.” The one who owned everything emptied himself, was born with nowhere to lay his head, died stripped of even his garments — so that bankrupt men could inherit the unsearchable riches of Christ.

So this week, when the Word follows your treasure and exposes where your heart has actually gone, do not despair and do not rationalize. Bring the divided heart to the One who became poor to make you rich. You will not dethrone money by gritting your teeth; you will dethrone it by seeing a better treasure. Ask the Spirit to open your eyes to the surpassing worth of Christ, until the riches that rot lose their grip and your heart follows its true treasure home. The man who sees the emptiness of earthly treasure and the fullness of Christ is being revived — from the dust of a divided heart to a heart whose treasure is the Lord, and whose riches can never be lost.

stations.verse: Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
stations.question: If I follow my money and my daydreams, where do they say my heart actually is — on earth, or in heaven?
stations.gloss: treasure, a store of what one values most
stations.live: Trace your treasure this week — your spending, your daydreams, your fears of loss — and you will find your heart. Then ask God to make Christ the treasure your heart follows home.
body: Thēsauros is a treasure store — the place where a person keeps what he values most. Jesus says the location of your thēsauros determines the location of your heart: the heart follows the treasure, not the other way around. This is the searching diagnostic. A man cannot simply will his heart to love God more; but he can examine where his treasure goes, and there he will find his heart. The cure is not to scold the heart but to relocate the treasure — to find Christ more valuable than gold.

stations.verse: No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.
stations.question: Jesus says I serve one master or the other, not both. When God and money have pulled in opposite directions, which one has actually won?
stations.gloss: mammon, wealth personified as a rival master
stations.live: Stop imagining a truce between God and money. Name which has been your master, and ask Christ to take the throne money has been sitting on.
body: Mamōnas is wealth treated as a power — not just coins but money as a rival lord competing for the throne of the heart. Jesus personifies it deliberately, because money is never neutral; it presses to be served, to be trusted, to be obeyed. It makes a useful servant and a tyrannical master. The heart has room for one lord on its throne, and the question is never whether you will serve a master, but which master owns you.

stations.verse: The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!
stations.question: Jesus says a grasping eye darkens the whole man. Where has greed for more spread its shadow over my peace, my relationships, my worship?
stations.gloss: simple, single, undivided
stations.live: Watch where your eye goes when money comes up this week — the balance, the purchase, the other man’s house. Ask the Father for a single eye.
body: The WEB renders it “sound.” The lexicon’s sense is simple, single. The single eye is not looking two ways at once, part at God and part at the pile. Scripture already set its opposite, the evil eye, against the closed hand of a man who will not give to his poor brother. The single eye is the undivided heart looking out, and it is always an open-handed eye. You cannot serve two masters. Your eye cannot fix on two treasures.

stations.verse: But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
stations.question: The desire to be rich is named a snare. Where has the craving for more lured me into compromise I would not otherwise have made?

stations.verse: He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.
stations.question: My life does not consist in what I own — yet I often live as if it does. Where am I measuring my life by my possessions?
stations.gloss: covetousness, the greedy craving for more
stations.live: Name the “if I just had a little more” lie you keep believing. Contentment is not one more acquisition away; it is found in Christ, who is already yours.
body: Pleonexia is the itch for more — literally a grasping to have more than one has, a craving never satisfied by acquisition. Paul calls it idolatry, because it sets the heart’s trust and longing on possessions in the place of God. It is the engine under the divided heart: not the having of money but the endless wanting of it. And it can never be fed into contentment; only a heart that has found its treasure in Christ is freed from the grasping for more.

stations.verse: Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.
stations.question: Contentment is grounded in God’s promise never to leave me, not in my balance. Do I seek security in his presence or in my provision?
stations.gloss: without love of money, not covetous
stations.live: When the fear of not having enough tightens your grip this week, say Hebrews 13:5 out loud. Then give something away.
body: It is the negative of the word Luke uses for the Pharisees who “were lovers of money” and scoffed at Jesus. Hebrews commands the free man — free from the love of money, content with what he has. But look at the reason given. Not a budget. A promise: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” A man grips money because he is afraid of being left with nothing. The cure for the grip is the God who will not leave.

stations.verse: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.
stations.question: Christ became poor to make me rich in him. How does that gift loosen money’s grip and reset what I count as wealth?

stations.verse: Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field.
stations.question: The man sold everything with joy because he saw the treasure’s worth. Do I see Christ as a treasure worth gladly letting everything else go?

stations.verse: Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
stations.question: Paul counted all his wealth as loss next to knowing Christ. What am I still counting as gain that I need to see beside the surpassing worth of Christ?
pulls: You will not dethrone money by gritting your teeth. You dethrone it by seeing a better treasure — Christ himself.

practices.title: FOLLOW YOUR TREASURE TO FIND YOUR HEART
practices.body: Jesus says your heart follows your treasure, so this week, trace the trail honestly. Look at where your money goes without a struggle, what you daydream about, what loss would devastate you, where your mood rises and falls. Write down what you find. Then hold it next to Matthew 6:21 and let it tell you the truth about where your heart actually is. You cannot bring a divided heart to Christ until you have honestly located it.

practices.title: NAME MONEY’S PLACE ON THE THRONE
practices.body: You cannot serve two masters, so name which one has been winning. This week, identify the specific ways money has acted as your master — the security you seek in it, the anxiety when it is threatened, the compromises made for it. Confess it plainly: “Lord, money has been on the throne of my heart, and you cannot share it. Take the place it has been holding.” Naming the rival master is the first step to dethroning it.

practices.title: LOOSEN GREED WITH GENEROSITY
practices.body: The sound, single eye is a generous one, and generosity is how a man pries greed’s fingers loose. This week, give — deliberately, sacrificially, beyond the comfortable — and notice how giving loosens money’s grip in a way that resolving never does. Pray as you give: “Lord, I give this to prove that you, not money, are my treasure, and to ask you to free my grasping heart.” Generosity is not just duty; it is therapy for a heart enslaved to wealth.

practices.title: LOOK TO THE ONE WHO BECAME POOR
practices.body: You will not loosen money’s hold by white-knuckling detachment; you loosen it by seeing a greater treasure. This week, dwell on the One who, though rich, became poor for you — who emptied himself into your poverty to make you rich in him. Pray it: “Lord, you became a beggar to make me wealthy in you. Open my eyes to riches that rot cannot touch.” A man freed by the riches of Christ no longer needs money to be his god.

practices.title: TELL A BROTHER WHERE MONEY OWNS YOU
practices.body: Money’s mastery thrives in privacy, dressed up as prudence so it never has to be confessed. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother one specific way money has owned your heart, and ask him to help you keep Christ on the throne. The idol that can be served respectably and in secret is broken when it is finally named out loud to another man.

title: Treasure and the Divided Heart
subtitle: from dust to treasure that lasts
keyVerse: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. … No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

passage.text: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON TREASURE AND THE HEART
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling detached from money by Friday. It is about following your treasure to find your heart, bringing the divided heart to the One who became poor for you, and asking the Spirit to make Christ your greatest treasure.
prayer: Father, my heart has followed my money. I have looked at the balance more than I have looked at you. I cannot pry my own fingers loose. Lord Jesus, you were rich and became poor for my sake. You are the treasure moth and rust cannot touch. Holy Spirit, give me a single eye and an open hand, and let me give something away today with a light heart.
prayerLines: Father, my heart has followed my money.
I have looked at the balance more than I have looked at you.
I cannot pry my own fingers loose.
Lord Jesus, you were rich and became poor for my sake.
You are the treasure moth and rust cannot touch.
Holy Spirit, give me a single eye and an open hand,
and let me give something away today with a light heart.
bottomLine: Matthew 6:19–24 exposes the one idol a man can serve openly and still be admired — money — and refuses any truce between it and God. Your heart follows your treasure, Jesus says, so the trail of your money and your daydreams reveals the master you actually serve. No man dethrones money by willpower, because the heart simply re-enthrones it. But there is one who, though rich, became poor for your sake, that you through his poverty might become rich — and a heart that sees the surpassing worth of Christ is freed from the riches that rot. The way out of the divided heart is not tighter detachment. It is to follow your treasure honestly, bring the divided heart to the One who became poor for you, and let the Spirit make Christ the treasure your heart follows home.
benediction: Brother, of all the idols the dust offers you, money is the most respectable — the one you can serve in plain sight and be praised for serving. And precisely because it dresses as prudence, it has likely held more of your heart than you have ever admitted. Jesus has held up the mirror and told you to follow your treasure, and the trail has led somewhere uncomfortable: to the anxiety, the grasping, the security sought in a number, the heart that says it serves God while quietly bowing to mammon. Lift your eyes off the rotting hoard.

When you catch your heart following its treasure to the wrong place this week, lift up your eyes. When the fear of not having enough grips you, lift up your eyes. When you feel money’s pull to the throne that belongs to God alone, lift up your eyes to the One who owned everything and gave it all away. Jesus, though he was rich with all the riches of heaven, became poor for your sake — born in a borrowed stable, with nowhere to lay his head, dying stripped of even his clothes — so that you, bankrupt and grasping, might become rich with riches that moth and rust and thief and death can never touch. He became a beggar to make you an heir.

This is from dust to revival — not a man wrenching his fingers off his money by sheer willpower, but a man whose eyes have been opened to a treasure so much greater that the riches that rot lose their grip on him. You cannot serve God and money, but you were never meant to serve money at all; you were meant to be free of it, rich in Christ, your treasure safe in heaven where your heart can finally rest. Lift up your eyes to the One who became poor to make you rich, and let him be the treasure your heart follows all the way home.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of treasure that rots in your hands. But Christ became poor to make you rich in him. Lift up your eyes — your treasure is safe in heaven.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop serving money this week, and to find in Christ — who became poor to make you rich — a treasure so great that your divided heart is finally made whole?

sections.heading: The Sin You Never Confess
pulls: A man will confess anger and lust long before he thinks to confess worry. But underneath the worry is a quiet question about his Father.
paras: Anxiety is a sin almost no man confesses, because almost every man considers it normal, even responsible. Anxiety. The churning mind at two in the morning, the running of the numbers, the rehearsing of disasters that have not happened and may never happen, the low constant hum of worry about provision, health, the future, the children. A man will confess anger and lust before he ever thinks to confess worry, because worry feels less like sin and more like simply taking life seriously. But three times in this passage Jesus says the same thing: do not be anxious. He treats it not as a personality trait but as something to be put off.

Why does Jesus speak to anxiety so directly and so gently at once? Because he sees what it really is. Underneath a man’s worry is a question about his Father — whether God is truly good, truly able, truly attentive to a man’s needs. Anxiety is, at bottom, a quiet unbelief, a practical doubt that the Father who clothes the grass and feeds the birds will actually care for his own child. Jesus does not shame the anxious man; he reasons with him, tenderly, pointing him to a Father whose care is the cure for every fear.

sections.heading: Anxiety Is a Question About the Father
paras: The whole logic of this passage turns on one word Jesus keeps using: Father. Look at the birds — your heavenly Father feeds them. Consider the lilies — your Father clothes them. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Jesus does not cure anxiety by telling a man to think positively or to manage his stress. He cures it by changing the man’s vision of God, from a distant force a man must wrest provision from, to a Father who already knows, already cares, and already feeds his children. The cure for worry is not a technique. It is a Father.

And here the mirror shows a man something humbling: his anxiety has been a measure of his unbelief. Every sleepless night of worry has been, in a sense, a vote of no confidence in his Father’s goodness and power. This is not said to heap guilt on an already burdened man, but to send him to the only real remedy. If worry is unbelief, then the cure is not trying harder to stop worrying — which only adds anxiety about being anxious — but coming to know and trust the Father better. The anxious man does not need more willpower. He needs more Father.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Look at the Birds, Consider the Lilies
paras: Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater. “See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them.” Consider the lilies of the field: they do not labor or spin, and yet not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of them. If God lavishes such care on birds that do not worry and flowers that do not last, how much more will he care for his own children, made in his image, bought by his Son? The argument is meant to disarm a man’s fear with the sheer evidence of the Father’s daily, visible care for creatures far less valuable than he.

Notice that Jesus tells a man to look and to consider — to stop and actually observe the Father’s care written across the natural world. Anxiety keeps a man’s eyes locked on his problems, spiraling inward. Jesus lifts the eyes outward and upward, to the fed birds and the clothed fields, as daily sermons on the Father’s faithfulness. The cure begins with where a man looks. The worrier stares at the threat; the believing son looks at the birds and remembers his Father feeds them, and that he is worth far more than they.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Worry Changes Nothing, and Misreads the Father
paras: Jesus asks a piercing question: “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?” Worry is not only unbelief; it is futility. It changes nothing it frets about. It cannot add an hour, cannot pay a bill, cannot heal a body, cannot secure a future. It only steals today’s peace to spend on tomorrow’s troubles, most of which never arrive. The anxious man pours out his strength on a thing that accomplishes nothing except to rob him of the present and dishonor the Father who holds the future.

And Jesus names whose pattern this is: the Gentiles, those without a Father, seek after all these things. The pagan worries because he has no one over him who cares; he must secure his own life because no one else will. But the child of God is not an orphan scrambling for provision in an indifferent universe. He has a Father who knows exactly what he needs before he asks. To worry as the world worries is to live as a practical orphan, forgetting the Father at one’s side. The believing son worries differently, or learns not to, because he is not alone.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Seek First the Kingdom
paras: Then comes the great reorientation: “seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” Jesus does not merely tell a man to stop worrying; he gives him something greater to pursue. The anxious heart is a heart that has made the wrong thing first — food, clothing, security, the lesser things — and so it churns over them endlessly. The cure is to put first things first: to seek the kingdom and the righteousness of God above all, and to trust the Father to add the rest. A heart fixed on the kingdom has less room for the worries that consume a heart fixed on itself.

And notice the righteousness Jesus says to seek — the righteousness that, as this whole study has insisted, a man cannot produce and must receive in Christ. Even the cure for anxiety runs through the gospel. The man who seeks first the kingdom is the man who has stopped trying to secure his own life and standing, and has rested both in his Father. He seeks God’s righteousness, found in Christ, and entrusts his daily needs to the Father’s hand. Anxiety loosens its grip not when a man tries to relax, but when he reorders his loves and rests his whole life in the Father.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Care of the Father
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for an anxious man, churning at two in the morning, is this: you have a Father who feeds the birds and clothes the fields, and you are worth more to him than all of them. The proof is not a promise of an easy life but the cross itself. The Father “who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” — how would he not also, with him, freely give you all you truly need? The God who gave you Christ when you were his enemy will not abandon you now that you are his child.

So this week, when the familiar worry rises and the mind begins to churn, do not merely try to stop it, and do not excuse it as responsible. Take it to your Father as the quiet unbelief it is, and let him answer it — with the birds, with the lilies, with the cross where he proved his care forever. Seek first his kingdom, rest your needs in his hands, and look up from your problems to the Father who already knows them all. The man who casts his anxiety on the Father and seeks first the kingdom is being revived — from the dust of churning fear to the rest of a child who knows he is fed, clothed, and held by a Father who counts him precious.

stations.verse: Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they?
stations.question: Jesus points me to the fed birds as proof of the Father’s care. What worry am I carrying that his question — “Aren’t you of much more value than they?” — would answer?
stations.gloss: to be anxious, to be pulled apart by care
stations.live: When you feel your mind pulling apart over tomorrow, name it as merimna and bring the scattered pieces to your Father. He holds the future that is tearing you in two.
body: Merimnaō pictures a mind pulled in pieces, divided and distracted by care — the very fragmentation a worried man feels. Jesus uses it repeatedly here, treating anxiety not as a harmless habit but as something to be put off. The word exposes what worry does: it tears a man apart, scattering his peace across a hundred tomorrows. And the cure is not to suppress the pieces by force but to gather the divided heart back onto one thing — the Father who holds every tomorrow already.

stations.verse: Which of you, by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?
stations.question: Worry changes nothing it frets about. What am I pouring my strength into worrying over that my anxiety is powerless to alter?
stations.gloss: age, span of life; stature
stations.live: Name the thing you have worried over most this week. Ask plainly: what has all that worry added? Then hand it to the Father who feeds the birds.
body: Hēlikia can mean a man’s age or his height — the same word describes Zacchaeus, too short to see over the crowd. Translators split on which sense Jesus means here. It does not change the point. Worry cannot add a moment to your life or an inch to your frame. All that churning, and nothing gets added. The only thing worry grows is the worry.

stations.verse: Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.
stations.question: The Father already knows my needs. Am I living like a child whose Father knows, or like an orphan who must secure everything alone?
stations.gloss: to seek after, to crave, to chase anxiously
stations.live: Catch yourself chasing provision like an orphan this week, and remember you have a Father who already knows. Redirect the chase: seek first his kingdom, and trust him with the rest.
body: Epizēteō is to seek intently, to chase after — Jesus says the Gentiles, those without a Father, epizēteō the basics of life because they must secure their own existence in an indifferent world. The same verb returns in verse 33, redirected: seek first the kingdom. The chasing is not killed but reaimed. The orphan chases provision because no one cares for him; the child is freed to chase the kingdom because his Father has already taken responsibility for his needs.

stations.verse: But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
stations.question: An anxious heart has made the wrong thing first. What lesser thing have I been seeking first, and what would it mean to seek the kingdom instead?

stations.verse: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
stations.question: I borrow tomorrow’s troubles and carry them today. Where am I living in a future the Father has not yet given me grace for?

stations.verse: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time, casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
stations.question: I am invited to cast all my worries on him because he cares. What specific worry do I need to hand over to the Father this week?
stations.gloss: to throw upon, to cast off onto another
stations.live: Worry is a weight you were never meant to carry. This week, name a specific anxiety and deliberately throw it onto the Father — he cares for you and is strong enough to hold it.
body: Epiriptō means to fling or throw something onto another — the same word used for throwing garments onto the colt Jesus rode. Peter pictures anxiety as a weight a man takes off himself and hurls onto God, because God cares for him. It is decisive, not gradual: a deliberate casting of the load onto the One strong enough to carry it. The anxious man is not told to carry his worry better, but to throw it off entirely onto a Father who has already shouldered it.

stations.verse: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: The antidote to anxiety in this verse is thankful prayer. Am I turning my worries into prayers, or just turning them over and over in my mind?
stations.gloss: to guard, to keep under guard
stations.live: When worry comes to the door at night this week, pray Philippians 4:6 — and then leave the watch to the One who keeps it.
body: Paul uses this word for the governor of Damascus guarding the city gates to catch him. It is a watchman’s word, a man posted on the wall. The peace of God, “which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” Peter uses it the same way: you are “guarded through faith” by the power of God. You are not the one standing watch over your own heart through the night. God posts the guard.

stations.verse: He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?
stations.question: The Father proved his care by giving his Son. How does the cross settle, once for all, the question of whether he will provide what I truly need?

stations.verse: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
stations.question: My Father gives good gifts more readily than the best earthly father. Do I approach him expecting good, or braced for disappointment?
pulls: The anxious man does not need more willpower. He needs more Father.

practices.title: NAME THE WORRY AS UNBELIEF, GENTLY
practices.body: Most men excuse anxiety as responsibility and never bring it to God as sin. This week, name your specific worry honestly, and name what it says about your Father — that you doubt he is good enough, able enough, or attentive enough to care for you. Write it down. Then write across it Matthew 6:26: “Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they?” This is not to heap on guilt, but to send the worry to its only real cure — a better knowledge of your Father.

practices.title: LOOK AT THE BIRDS, ON PURPOSE
practices.body: Jesus says to look and to consider — anxiety locks the eyes on the problem, so the cure begins by lifting them. This week, deliberately look: at the birds the Father feeds, the provision already in your life, the prayers he has already answered. When the churning starts, physically lift your eyes from the threat to the evidence of his care. Train yourself to read creation as the daily sermon on the Father’s faithfulness that Jesus says it is.

practices.title: CAST IT — DON’T CARRY IT
practices.body: Peter says to throw your anxiety onto God, decisively, not to manage it better. This week, when a worry rises, do not turn it over and over; name it and cast it: “Father, this is too heavy for me, and you care for me. I throw it onto you.” Make it a definite act of handing the weight over, as real as setting down a load. You were never meant to carry tomorrow; the Father already holds it.

practices.title: TURN WORRY INTO PRAYER
practices.body: Paul gives the exchange directly: do not be anxious, but in everything, by prayer with thanksgiving, make your requests known. This week, every time you catch yourself worrying, convert the worry into a prayer on the spot — ask, and give thanks for what God has already done. The same mental energy that fuels anxiety can fuel petition. Pray your worries instead of rehearsing them, and let the peace of God guard your heart.

practices.title: ANCHOR IN THE CROSS WHEN PROVISION FEELS UNCERTAIN
practices.body: When the future feels genuinely frightening, the dust says God may not come through. Reverse it with the cross. This week, when provision feels uncertain, preach Romans 8:32 to yourself: “The Father gave his own Son for me when I was his enemy. He will not abandon me now that I am his child.” The God who gave you Christ has already settled the question of his care; rest your unknown future in the hands that were pierced for you. Tell a brother the worry, and ask him to remind you of the cross.

title: The Cure for Anxiety
subtitle: from dust to the care of the Father

Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they?

Lord Jesus, the Father did not spare you for me.
He will not forget me now.
Holy Spirit, when the worry comes at night, turn it into prayer,
and set your peace on guard over my heart.
bottomLine: Matthew 6:25–34 speaks to the sin a man never confesses — anxiety — and names it for what it is: a quiet unbelief about whether the Father is good, able, and attentive. The cure is not a technique or more willpower, which only adds worry about worrying. The cure is a Father, who feeds the birds, clothes the fields, knows your needs before you ask, and counts you worth far more than the creatures he already cares for. He proved it at the cross, where he gave his own Son for his enemies. The way out of churning fear is not to try harder to relax. It is to seek first his kingdom, cast your anxiety on him, and rest your whole life in the care of the Father who gave you Christ.
benediction: Brother, the dust does its quietest work at two in the morning, when the house is still and the mind begins to churn — running the numbers, rehearsing the disasters, carrying tomorrow’s troubles into tonight’s darkness. You have probably never thought of that churning as sin; it feels like simply taking life seriously. But Jesus, gently, names it for what it is: a quiet unbelief, a doubt about whether your Father is good enough and strong enough to care for his own child. And he does not shame you for it. He reasons with you, tenderly, and lifts your eyes off your fears.

When the worry rises this week, lift up your eyes — to the birds of the sky your Father feeds without their sowing or reaping. When the future frightens you, lift up your eyes — to the lilies of the field he clothes more gloriously than Solomon. When provision feels uncertain and the churning will not stop, lift up your eyes to the cross, where your Father settled the question of his care forever. He “who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” — delivered him up for you, when you were his enemy. How would he not, with him, give you everything you truly need? The God who gave you Christ will not now abandon you over your daily bread.

This is from dust to revival — not a man mastering his anxiety by sheer technique, but a man who has come to know his Father so well that the worry loses its grip. You are not an orphan, scrambling to secure your life in an indifferent universe. You are a child, fed and clothed and held by a Father who knows your every need before you speak it and counts you precious beyond the birds and the flowers. Seek first his kingdom, cast every anxiety onto him, and lift up your eyes from your churning fears to the Father who has never once failed to care for his own. Rest, child. He has you.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust and churns with fear at two in the morning. But your Father feeds the birds and gave his Son for you. Lift up your eyes — he has you.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop carrying tomorrow’s worry this week, and to rest as a child in the care of the Father who feeds the birds and gave his own Son for you?

sections.heading: The Sin With Perfect Vision for Everyone Else
pulls: The human heart has eagle-eyed vision for the faults of others and near-total blindness to its own.
paras: There is a strange optical condition the human heart suffers from: perfect, eagle-eyed vision for the faults of others, and near-total blindness to its own. A man can spot the smallest flaw in his neighbor — the speck, the splinter, the petty failing — while a beam, a great timber, juts out of his own eye unnoticed. He is harsh with others and gentle with himself, quick to judge and slow to examine, an expert prosecutor of everyone but the one man he knows best. Jesus draws the picture so absurdly that a man cannot miss it: someone fumbling at a speck in another’s eye while a plank protrudes from his own.

This is the sin Jesus exposes here, and it is one of the most respectable and self-righteous of all. The critical, judging spirit feels like discernment, like a commitment to standards, like caring about what is right. But Jesus calls the speck-inspector a hypocrite, because the same standard he wields against others would bury him if turned around. The man with the beam has no business performing surgery on specks. The Word holds up a mirror and shows a man not his neighbor’s faults, which he sees so clearly, but his own, which he has somehow managed never to notice.

sections.heading: The Measure You Use Returns to You
paras: Jesus attaches a sobering principle: “with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.” The standard a man applies to others is the standard that will be applied to him. The harsh, ungracious, nitpicking measure he metes out will come back upon his own head. This is not a call to abandon all moral discernment — Jesus is not forbidding the recognition of right and wrong — but a warning against the censorious heart that loves to condemn, that finds a grim satisfaction in others’ failures, that exalts itself by lowering everyone else.

And here the mirror does its deepest work, because a judging spirit is finally a failure to see oneself rightly. The man who truly saw the beam in his own eye — the depth of his own sin before a holy God — could never be so harsh about the specks in others. His severity toward others is the precise measure of his blindness toward himself. The cure, then, is not merely to stop criticizing, but to see clearly: to face the beam, to be undone by one’s own sin first, and from that honest, humbled place to deal gently and mercifully with others.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: First the Log, Then the Speck
paras: Notice carefully what Jesus does and does not say. He does not say the speck in the brother’s eye is nothing, or that it never needs removing. He says, “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” There is an order, and the order is everything. Self-examination comes before the examination of others. A man earns the right to help with his brother’s speck only by first dealing honestly and humbly with his own beam. The problem was never that he noticed the speck; it was that he noticed it while ignoring his beam.

This is the rhythm the whole sermon has been training: always see your own sin before you see another’s. The man who has truly reckoned with his own heart — its anger, its lust, its greed, its pride, all the sermon has exposed — approaches his brother’s faults entirely differently. He comes not as a prosecutor but as a fellow patient, not to condemn but to help, gently, knowing his own desperate need of the same mercy. Clear sight of self produces gentle hands with others. The man undone by his own beam handles specks with care.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Mercy, Because You Have Received Mercy
paras: Behind the call to stop judging lies the deepest logic of the gospel: a man extends mercy because he has received it. The servant in Jesus’ parable who was forgiven an unpayable debt and then seized his fellow servant by the throat over a trifling one is the very picture of the speck-inspector. Having been forgiven everything, he showed mercy in nothing — and his master was rightly enraged. The man who knows the size of the debt he has been forgiven cannot then be harsh about the small debts others owe him. Mercy received, truly received, overflows into mercy given.

This is why a judging spirit is, at root, a gospel problem. The harsh, critical man has not felt the weight of his own forgiveness. If he had — if he had stood, beam and all, before a holy God and received pardon he could never earn — he could not turn around and condemn his brother’s speck. Blessed are the merciful, Jesus said, for they shall receive mercy. The flow runs both ways: the one who has received mercy becomes merciful, and the merciful go on receiving the mercy they extend. To grow gentle with others, a man must go deeper into the mercy he has been shown.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The One Who Was Judged in Your Place
paras: Here the gospel rises to answer the judging heart at its root. Jesus, the only man with no beam and no speck — the only one who ever had the right to judge — did not come to condemn. And then he, the sinless Judge, stepped into the place of the guilty and was himself judged. He stood silent before unjust judges, was condemned by the very men he had the right to condemn, and bore on the cross the full judgment that every harsh, sinful heart deserves. The one with perfect vision and perfect standing took the verdict that belonged to beams and specks alike, so that condemned men could go free.

And this changes everything about how a forgiven man treats his brother. The judgment you feared has already fallen — on Christ, in your place — so you no longer need to secure your standing by lowering everyone else. The man resting in Christ’s finished work has nothing to prove and no verdict to dread, and so he is freed to be merciful, to deal gently, to help with specks instead of condemning over them. The cross both humbles a man, showing him the beam Christ had to bear, and frees him, removing the judgment he was trying to escape by judging others.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to Mercy
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man whose critical, judging heart has just been exposed is this: you have a beam of your own, and Christ bore the judgment for it, so that you might extend to others the mercy you received. You are not the prosecutor; you are the pardoned. The honest sight of your own sin, far from crushing you, frees you — because the judgment it deserves has already fallen on Christ, and what remains for you is mercy, both to receive and to give.

So this week, when you catch your eagle eye fixed on a brother’s speck, do not merely try to stop criticizing. Turn the gaze around. Face your own beam first, let it humble you, and remember the cross where your judgment was carried. From that honest, grateful, humbled place, deal with others as one who has been shown enormous mercy and is glad to show it. The man who sees his own beam, rests in the cross, and grows merciful toward others is being revived — from the dust of a harsh and judging heart to the freedom of the pardoned, who handle their brothers’ specks with the gentle hands of the forgiven.

stations.verse: Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.
stations.question: The measure I use on others returns to me. Would I survive the standard I have been applying to the people around me?
stations.gloss: to judge, to condemn, to pass sentence
stations.live: Before you pass sentence on someone this week, ask whether you could survive that same verdict. The measure you use is the measure you invite onto your own head.
body: Krinō can mean simply to discern, but here it carries the weight of condemnation — to pass sentence, to set oneself up as judge over another. Jesus is not forbidding all moral discernment; he is forbidding the censorious heart that loves to condemn. The chilling principle is that the standard a man wields becomes the standard he is measured by. The one who sets himself on the judgment seat will find himself in the dock, judged by the very measure he was so eager to apply to others.

stations.verse: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
stations.question: I see specks clearly and miss my own beam entirely. What beam in my own eye have I been ignoring while inspecting others?
stations.gloss: a beam, a beam, a heavy plank of timber
stations.live: Assume the beam is yours before you go looking for specks. Ask God to show you the beam everyone else can see and you somehow cannot.
body: Dokos is a load-bearing beam, a massive plank of timber — the deliberate absurdity is the point. Jesus pictures a man with a structural beam jutting from his eye, squinting to extract a tiny splinter from someone else’s. The image exposes the comic, tragic blindness of the judging heart: the very sin that makes a man harsh is the one he cannot see in himself. The beam is not a small flaw but a great one, obvious to everyone but the man who carries it.

stations.verse: You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
stations.question: Jesus does not say ignore the speck, but deal with my beam first. Where do I need to examine myself before I address anyone else?

stations.verse: Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things.
stations.question: I often condemn in others what I practice myself. What sin am I harshest about in others that lives, quietly, in me?
stations.gloss: without excuse, inexcusable
stations.live: The next time you pass sentence on someone in your head this week, stop and ask: would I survive that same verdict? Then thank Christ that you do not have to.
body: This was a courtroom term: a man with no defense left to offer. Paul springs it on the judging man. The moment you condemn another, you have admitted you know the standard — and you break it yourself. Your own verdict on your brother becomes the evidence against you. There is only one way out of that courtroom. Not a better defense. A Substitute who took the sentence.

stations.verse: Then his lord called him in, and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt, because you begged me. Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
stations.question: I have been forgiven an unpayable debt. Whose small debt against me am I clutching as if I had never been forgiven my own?
stations.gloss: to have pity or mercy on, to show mercy
stations.live: Name the small debt you are refusing to release. Set it beside the mountain you have been forgiven, and show the mercy you were shown.
body: “Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” The king’s question uses this verb twice. The mercy you received is the measure of the mercy you owe. It is the same word behind the beatitude: the merciful “shall obtain mercy.” Mercy is not a mood a man works up toward people who deserve it. It is what flows out of a man who remembers the debt that was cancelled for him.

stations.verse: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.
stations.question: Mercy given and mercy received flow together. Where is my lack of mercy toward others cutting me off from the mercy I long to feel?

stations.verse: Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge. Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?
stations.question: There is one Judge, and it is not me. Where have I climbed onto a judgment seat that belongs to God alone?

stations.verse: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
stations.question: The one with every right to condemn came to save instead. How should the mercy of the only rightful Judge reshape the way I treat others?

stations.verse: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
stations.question: The goal is to restore gently, watching myself — not to condemn. When I see a brother’s fault, is my instinct to restore him or to feel above him?
stations.gloss: to mend, repair; to restore, make complete
stations.live: If you must address a brother’s fault this week, come to mend, not to win. Ask first: what would it take to make this net whole again?
body: Matthew uses this word for James and John in the boat, mending their nets. That is the picture Paul reaches for when a brother is caught in a fault. You are not a prosecutor gathering evidence. You are a fisherman with a torn net in your lap — patient, careful, working the knots back into place so the net can be used again. And Paul adds the warning every mender needs: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”
pulls: The man undone by his own beam handles his brother’s specks with the gentle hands of the forgiven.

practices.title: TEST THE MEASURE YOU USE
practices.body: Jesus says the measure you use returns to you, so this week, examine it. Whom have you been harsh about, and what standard have you been applying? Write it down, then ask honestly: could I survive that same verdict? Hold it next to Matthew 7:2. Seeing that your own measure would condemn you is the beginning of trading the judgment seat for the place of the pardoned.

practices.title: GO LOOKING FOR YOUR OWN LOG
practices.body: The man with the beam is the last to see it, so this week, go looking on purpose. Ask God to show you the beam everyone else can see and you somehow cannot — the obvious sin you have been excusing while inspecting others’ specks. Pray Psalm 139: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Show me the beam in my own eye.” You cannot remove a beam you refuse to look for.

practices.title: SET THE SPECK BESIDE YOUR FORGIVEN DEBT
practices.body: When you catch yourself clutching someone’s small offense, do what the unforgiving servant would not. This week, set the speck beside the mountain you have been forgiven in Christ: “Lord, I am holding this small debt against my brother while you have released me from an unpayable one.” Let the size of your own pardon shrink the offense in your hand until you can release it the way you were released.

practices.title: RESTORE GENTLY, FROM THE PLACE OF THE PARDONED
practices.body: Jesus does not say ignore the speck — he says deal with your beam first, then help with the speck, gently. This week, if you must address a real fault in someone, come not as a prosecutor but as a fellow patient: humbled by your own beam, resting in the cross, aiming to restore rather than condemn. Pray it: “Lord, let me help my brother the way you have helped me — gently, mercifully, as one forgiven much.”

practices.title: CONFESS YOUR JUDGING HEART TO A BROTHER
practices.body: A critical spirit hides behind the mask of discernment and rarely gets confessed as sin. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother where you have been harsh and judging, and ask him to point out the beams you cannot see and to remind you how much you have been forgiven. It takes humility to ask another man to help you see your own beam — and that humility is the beginning of mercy.
