stationsLabel: THE WORD ON JUDGMENT AND MERCY
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about achieving a non-judgmental attitude by Friday. It is about facing your own beam, resting in the cross where your judgment fell, and from that humbled place extending the mercy you have received.
prayer: Father, I have judged my brother harshly and excused myself freely. I have inspected specks with a beam in my own eye. I would not survive the verdict I passed on him. Lord Jesus, you were judged in my place. The sentence fell on you so I would go free. Holy Spirit, show me my own beam first, and give me gentle hands for my brother’s speck.
prayerLines: Father, I have judged my brother harshly and excused myself freely.
I have inspected specks with a beam in my own eye.
I would not survive the verdict I passed on him.
Lord Jesus, you were judged in my place.
The sentence fell on you so I would go free.
Holy Spirit, show me my own beam first,
and give me gentle hands for my brother’s speck.
bottomLine: Matthew 7:1–6 exposes the sin with perfect vision for everyone else and total blindness to itself — the harsh, judging heart that inspects specks while a beam juts from its own eye. The measure a man uses returns to him, and his severity toward others is the precise measure of his blindness toward himself. The cure is not merely to stop criticizing but to see rightly: to face your own beam, to be undone by your own sin, and to remember the cross where the only rightful Judge was judged in your place. The man who has received such mercy is freed to give it. The way out of a judging heart is not gritted-teeth tolerance. It is to face your beam, rest in the cross, and handle others’ specks with the gentle hands of the forgiven.
benediction: Brother, the dust has given you remarkable eyes — sharp enough to catch the smallest splinter in another man’s eye, while a great beam juts from your own, entirely unnoticed. The judging heart feels like discernment, like a love of standards, like caring about what is right. But Jesus holds up the mirror and shows you the absurd, tragic truth: you have been performing eye surgery on specks with a beam protruding from your own face, harsh with everyone but the one man you know best. Lift your eyes off your brother’s speck.

When you catch your eagle eye fixed on someone else’s fault this week, lift up your eyes. When the satisfaction of condemning rises in you, lift up your eyes. When you feel the urge to lower someone else to raise yourself, lift up your eyes to the only man who ever had the right to judge — and laid it down. Jesus, with no beam and no speck, the sinless Judge of all, did not come to condemn but to save. And then he stepped into the dock in your place, stood silent before unjust judges, and bore on the cross the full judgment your harsh and sinful heart deserved. The one with every right to condemn was condemned, so that you could go free.

This is from dust to revival — not a man gritting his teeth to tolerate others, but a man so humbled by his own beam and so freed by the cross that mercy begins to flow out of him. The judgment you feared has already fallen on Christ; you have nothing left to prove and no verdict left to dread. You are not the prosecutor. You are the pardoned — forgiven an unpayable debt — and the pardoned, when they truly grasp their pardon, cannot help becoming merciful. Lift up your eyes to the Judge who was judged for you, face your own beam in his light, and handle your brother’s specks with the gentle hands of a forgiven man.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust of a harsh and judging heart. But Christ, the only rightful Judge, was judged in your place. Lift up your eyes — the pardoned can a’ord to be merciful.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop inspecting the specks of others this week, and to face your own beam in the light of the cross — extending the mercy you have so freely received?

sections.heading: After the Demands, an Invitation
pulls: Asking is what a man does when he has -nally come to the end of himself. The self-su’icient never ask.
paras: By now the Sermon on the Mount has done its work. For chapter after chapter it has held up the mirror — exposing the anger, the lust, the crooked words, the loveless heart, the performing, the divided loyalty, the worry, the judging spirit — and it has set the bar at a perfection no man can reach. An honest man arrives here emptied, having given up every hope of climbing the mountain by his own strength. And it is precisely to that emptied man that Jesus now turns and says: ask. After all the demands, an invitation. After showing a man he cannot, Jesus tells him where to go for what he lacks.

This is no accident of arrangement. The command to ask, seek, and knock comes after the impossible standard, because asking is what a man does when he has finally come to the end of himself. The self-sufficient man does not ask; he provides for himself. Only the man who knows he is bankrupt — who has seen the beam in his eye, the lust in his heart, the perfection he cannot reach — is ready to do the one thing the whole sermon has been driving him toward: to stop striving and start asking, to come to the Father with empty hands and receive what he could never earn.

sections.heading: The Father Behind the Promise
paras: The promise is wide open: ask and it will be given, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened. But Jesus does not leave it as a bare promise; he grounds it in the character of the One being asked. What father, he says, if his son asks for bread, would give him a stone? “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” The whole confidence to ask rests not on the asker’s worthiness but on the Father’s goodness. Prayer is not prying gifts from a reluctant deity; it is a child asking a Father who delights to give.

And here the gospel holds up even your asking. A man can come to God with empty, bankrupt hands not because he has earned a hearing but because he has been made a son in Christ, and the Father loves to give good things to his children. The same grace that exposed his need now invites him to bring that need to a Father better than the best earthly father. The man who has despaired of himself is not left in despair; he is handed the most hopeful command in the sermon — ask — and pointed to a Father who answers.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Ask, Seek, Knock — the Posture of the Bankrupt
paras: Notice the progression and the persistence in Jesus’ words: ask, seek, knock. The tense is continuous — keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. This is not a single transaction but a settled posture, the ongoing dependence of a man who has learned he has nothing in himself and everything in his Father. The proud man asks for nothing because he admits no lack. The bankrupt man, who has been emptied by this sermon, becomes a lifelong asker, a perpetual seeker, a man forever knocking at the Father’s door — because he knows, now, where everything he needs is kept.

This is the very poverty of spirit the sermon began with, worked all the way through to its practical end. Blessed are the poor in spirit, Jesus said at the start; now, near the close, he tells the poor in spirit what to do with their poverty — bring it to the Father and ask. The whole Christian life turns out to be a life of holy begging, of coming again and again with empty hands to a Father who fills them. The man who has stopped trusting himself does not stop needing; he simply learns to ask, and to keep asking, all the way home.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Golden Rule and the Whole Law
paras: In the middle of this section Jesus places the Golden Rule: “whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.” In one sentence he sums up the entire ethical demand of Scripture toward other people — not a list of prohibitions, but a single, searching positive command to actively love others as you would want to be loved. And like everything else in the sermon, it exposes as much as it instructs, because no honest man can claim to have kept it. The standard of love it sets is the very standard the rest of the sermon has shown you constantly fail.

But place the Golden Rule next to the command to ask, and an order shows itself. A man cannot love others as he ought by sheer effort; he has proven that all sermon long. So what does he do? He asks. The love the Golden Rule requires is among the good gifts the Father gives to those who ask him. The command to treat others rightly drives a man, once again, not to self-reliance but to dependent prayer — to seek from the Father the love he cannot manufacture, so that he can begin, by grace, to give to others what he would want for himself.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The Narrow Gate and the Only Door
paras: Then Jesus turns to the gate: “Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it. How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.” The narrow gate is not a call to a harder version of self-effort; it is the opposite. The wide gate is the broad, comfortable road of every man making his own way, trusting his own righteousness, walking with the crowd. The narrow gate is so narrow that a man can bring nothing through it — not his record, not his merit, not his self-righteousness. He must drop everything and come through with empty hands.

And the narrow gate has a name. Jesus says elsewhere, “I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved.” The gate is narrow because there is only one of it — Christ himself, the only way to the Father, the one name under heaven by which a man is saved. The whole sermon has been narrowing a man down to this: away from the wide road of his own righteousness, down to the single narrow door of Christ. Few find it, because few will let go of themselves enough to enter. But the man who has been emptied by this sermon is finally ready to come through the only gate that opens onto life.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Open Door
paras: Psalm 119:25 cries from the floor: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And the reviving word for a man emptied by this sermon is this: there is a Father who gives good gifts to those who ask, and there is a narrow gate, already standing open, that leads to life. You are not left at the bottom of the mountain with a standard you cannot meet and no way up. You are invited to ask for everything you lack, and to enter the one door that was opened for you at the cost of Christ’s own body, broken to make a way through.

So this week, do the thing the whole sermon has been preparing you to do. Stop striving and start asking. Come to the Father with the empty hands the sermon has given you, and ask for the righteousness, the love, the mercy, the freedom you cannot produce. And enter, again, by the narrow gate — letting go of every shred of your own righteousness and coming through Christ alone. The man who has been emptied of himself and asks the Father, who enters by the one open door, is being revived — from the dust of his own bankrupt striving to the open hands of a child and the open door of the only gate that leads to life.

stations.verse: Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
stations.question: Asking is the posture of the bankrupt. Where am I still striving to provide for myself what I have never simply asked my Father to give?
stations.gloss: to ask, to request as one in need from one able to give
stations.live: Stop trying to manufacture what only the Father gives. Name the thing the sermon has exposed that you lack, and simply ask him for it — and keep asking.
body: Aiteō is the asking of a lesser to a greater — the request of a child to a father, a beggar to a benefactor, one who lacks to one who has. It is never the demand of an equal but the petition of need. Jesus commands this asking in the continuous tense: keep on asking. It is the settled posture of the man who has learned, through this whole sermon, that he has nothing in himself — and everything in the Father who delights to give to those who ask.

stations.verse: Or who is there among you, who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
stations.question: My confidence to ask rests on the Father’s goodness, not my worthiness. Do I picture him as eager to give, or reluctant and stingy?
stations.gloss: good, generous, bountiful in giving
stations.live: When you hesitate to ask God for something good, examine what you believe about his goodness. The Father is more eager to give good gifts than the best father you can imagine.
body: Agathos is goodness that overflows in benefit to others — not merely moral uprightness but active generosity. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: even flawed earthly fathers give good gifts; how much more will the perfectly agathos Father give good things to his children. The whole ground of bold asking is the goodness of the One asked. A man hesitates to ask only because he doubts the Father’s goodness; settle that, and the asking flows freely.

stations.verse: Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
stations.question: This one command sums up all I owe to others — and exposes how I fail it. Where am I treating others in ways I would never want done to me?

stations.verse: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?
stations.question: The Father gives the Spirit himself to those who ask. Am I asking for the greatest gift, or settling for asking only for lesser things?

stations.verse: Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it. How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.
stations.question: The narrow gate lets nothing of my own righteousness through. What am I still trying to carry through a gate that requires empty hands?
stations.gloss: narrow, confined, allowing little through
stations.live: The narrow gate admits no self-righteousness. Lay down everything you have been carrying as your own merit, and come through the one gate with empty hands.
body: Stenos means narrow, cramped, so confined that a man must leave things behind to pass. The narrow gate is not a stricter self-effort but a doorway too narrow for any baggage of self-righteousness, merit, or pride. A man comes through it only by dropping everything he was trusting in and entering with empty hands. It is narrow because there is only one way through — Christ alone — and few find it, because few will let go of themselves to enter.

stations.verse: I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved, and will go in and go out, and will find pasture.
stations.question: Jesus himself is the narrow gate. Am I trusting him as the only door, or still looking for some wider way that flatters my own efforts?
stations.gloss: a door
stations.live: When you pray this week, shut the door of the room behind you — and come in by the only Door that opens to the Father.
body: Thyra is the plain word for the door of a house — the one Jesus tells you to shut behind you when you pray in secret. Nothing mystical about it. Wood and hinge. And Jesus says, “I am the door. If anyone enters in by me, he will be saved.” The narrow gate of the sermon is not a technique or a level of devotion. It is a person. There is one way in, and he has a name.

stations.verse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
stations.question: There is one way to the Father, and it is a Person. Have I made peace with the narrowness of Christ as the only door, or do I resent it?

stations.verse: Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.
stations.question: I am invited to ask with confidence at the throne of grace. What keeps me approaching timidly when the door is already open?
stations.gloss: freedom in speaking, plainness, boldness, confidence
stations.live: Bring your request to God plainly this week — no preamble, no groveling, no pretending. You have been given the freedom to speak.
body: Parrēsia first meant freedom of speech — the right to speak plainly, with nothing held back. The Jewish leaders saw it in Peter and John, plain working men, and were amazed. Hebrews says you may “draw near with boldness to the throne of grace.” Not because you have earned a hearing. Because your High Priest is seated there. A beggar who knows the King’s Son speaks for him does not whisper at the door.

stations.verse: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
stations.question: God gives generously and without scolding to those who ask. What lack have I been hiding instead of simply bringing to him?
pulls: The whole sermon has been narrowing you down to a single door — away from your own righteousness, to Christ alone.

practices.title: TURN YOUR BANKRUPTCY INTO ASKING
practices.body: The sermon has emptied you; now bring the emptiness to the Father as a request. This week, take the specific thing the sermon has most exposed — the lust, the anger, the worry, the judging heart, the love you cannot produce — and instead of resolving to fix it, ask: “Father, I cannot manufacture this. I ask you for it.” Write down what you are asking for, and keep asking daily. Asking is the posture the whole sermon has been driving you toward.

practices.title: SETTLE THE QUESTION OF THE FATHER’S GOODNESS
practices.body: You hesitate to ask only because you doubt the Father’s heart. This week, when you find yourself reluctant to bring something to God, name the doubt and answer it with Matthew 7:11: “If earthly fathers give good gifts, how much more will my heavenly Father?” Picture him not as reluctant and stingy but as eager to give good things to his children. The bolder your view of his goodness, the freer your asking becomes.

practices.title: PRAY FOR THE LOVE THE GOLDEN RULE REQUIRES
practices.body: You cannot treat others as you wish to be treated by sheer willpower — so ask for it. This week, before each significant interaction, ask the Father for the very love the Golden Rule demands: “Lord, I cannot love this person as I would want to be loved. Give me what I lack.” Watch how the command to love others, which only exposed you before, becomes a doorway to dependent prayer and then to actual love.

practices.title: ENTER THE NARROW GATE AGAIN, WITH EMPTY HANDS
practices.body: The narrow gate admits no self-righteousness, and a man must keep entering it. This week, consciously lay down every shred of your own merit and come again through Christ alone: “Lord, I bring nothing of my own through this gate. You are the only door, and I enter by you.” Make it a daily act of letting go of yourself and resting wholly in Christ as the one way to the Father.

practices.title: ASK WITH A BROTHER
practices.body: What is hard to ask alone is easier asked together, and the sermon was never meant to be walked in isolation. Before the week ends, tell a trusted brother the specific thing you are asking the Father for, and ask him to keep asking alongside you. Two men knocking together at the Father’s door encourage each other to keep knocking until it opens — and remind each other that the door is Christ, and it is already open.

title: Ask, Seek, Knock, and the Narrow Gate
subtitle: from dust to the open door
keyVerse: Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you. … Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it.

passage.text: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
Or who is there among you, who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
“Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it.
How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON ASKING AND THE NARROW GATE
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about trying harder at the sermon’s demands. It is about doing what the whole sermon has prepared you for: coming to the Father with empty hands to ask, and entering the narrow gate that is Christ alone.
prayer: Father, I have tried to climb instead of ask. The sermon has shown me what I cannot produce. So I am asking — plainly, and again. Lord Jesus, you are the door. I come in by you, with empty hands. Holy Spirit, keep me asking, seeking, and knocking, and teach me to treat others the way I have been treated by grace.
prayerLines: Father, I have tried to climb instead of ask.
The sermon has shown me what I cannot produce.
So I am asking — plainly, and again.
Lord Jesus, you are the door.
I come in by you, with empty hands.
Holy Spirit, keep me asking, seeking, and knocking,
and teach me to treat others the way I have been treated by grace.
bottomLine: Matthew 7:7–14 turns, after all the sermon’s demands, to an invitation: ask, seek, knock. Asking is what a man does once he has come to the end of himself, and the whole sermon has been emptying him for exactly this. The promise rests not on the asker’s worth but on the Father’s goodness — a Father who gives good gifts, and the Spirit himself, to his children. Even the Golden Rule drives a man to ask for the love he cannot manufacture. And the narrow gate is no harder self-effort but the opposite: a door too narrow for any self-righteousness, with a single name — Christ, the only way to the Father. The way forward is not to climb the mountain at last. It is to come with empty hands, ask the good Father for what you lack, and enter the one open door that leads to life.
benediction: Brother, the sermon has spent chapter after chapter emptying you — exposing the anger and the lust and the worry and the judging heart, setting a bar of perfection no man alive could clear. If you have read it honestly, you have arrived here with nothing left in your hands, every hope of climbing the mountain by your own strength turned to dust. And it is exactly to that emptied man that Jesus turns and says the most hopeful word in the whole sermon: ask. After all the demands, an invitation. After showing you that you cannot, he tells you where to go for everything you lack. Lift your eyes off your empty hands.

When the sermon’s standard crushes you this week, lift up your eyes and ask. When you cannot produce the love or the purity or the peace it requires, lift up your eyes and ask. When you face the narrow gate and realize nothing of your own can come through it, lift up your eyes to the One who is himself the door. Jesus is the narrow gate, the one way to the Father, and the gate is narrow because there is only one of him — and his body was broken to open it. He stood in the wide road’s destination, bore it in your place, and became the single door that opens onto life, so that empty-handed men could come through and be saved.

This is from dust to revival — not a man finally scaling the mountain, but a man who has come to the end of himself and discovered a Father who gives good gifts to those who ask and a door already standing open. You do not enter the kingdom by your achievement; you enter by asking, by knocking, by coming through the one narrow gate with empty hands. Few find it, because few will let go of themselves enough to come. But you have been emptied for this very moment. Lift up your eyes to the good Father who answers and the open door who is Christ, and enter, child, by the only gate that leads to life.
closingVerse: Your soul clings to the dust with empty, bankrupt hands. But the Father gives good gifts to those who ask, and the door stands open. Lift up your eyes — and enter.
carry: Where is the Spirit inviting you to stop striving this week and simply ask — coming to the good Father with empty hands and entering, again, the one narrow gate that is Christ?

sections.heading: The End of the Road
pulls: The sermon ends where the whole study has been pointing: two houses, one storm, and the question of what you are built on.
paras: You have come to the last week of this study, and to the close of the sermon itself. For twelve weeks you have stood under the preaching of Jesus, and week by week it has done its appointed work — holding up the mirror, exposing the heart, setting a bar no man can reach, and driving you, again and again, off yourself and onto Christ. You began at the foot of the mountain with the verse that governed everything: “unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.” You have spent twelve weeks learning, sin by sin, that you do not have such a righteousness — and that Christ does, and gives it to those who are his.

Now Jesus ends his sermon as every wise preacher must: with a call to respond. He has shown you your heart; now he asks what you will build on. He has narrowed you down to a single door; now he asks whether you will come through it. The whole sermon comes to rest on one final image — two men, two houses, two foundations, and one storm that reveals what each was built on. It is the question the entire study has been pressing toward: when everything is shaken, what is your house actually founded on? Yourself, or the Rock?

sections.heading: Two Houses That Looked the Same
paras: The sobering thing about the parable is this: from the outside, the two houses may have looked identical. Both men heard the same words of Jesus. Both, perhaps, built structures that stood fine in fair weather. The difference was invisible until the storm came — the difference was the foundation, hidden underground, unseen until everything was tested. One had dug down to rock; the other had built on sand. And when the rain and floods and winds came, as they always come, one house stood and the other fell with a great crash. The foundation, not the appearance, was everything.

This is Jesus’ final warning against the very religion the whole sermon has exposed — the religion of the scribes and Pharisees, the religion of appearance without foundation, of hearing without the heart-deep response of faith. A man can hear every word of this sermon, admire it, even build a respectable-looking life on it, and still be building on sand if his foundation is his own righteousness rather than Christ. The storm — whether the storms of this life or the final storm of judgment — will reveal what no fair-weather inspection could. The only question that finally matters is the foundation.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Terror of “I Never Knew You”
paras: Just before the parable, Jesus speaks some of the most sobering words in all of Scripture. On the last day, he says, “Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’” These are not irreligious people. They are intensely religious — prophesying, casting out demons, working wonders, all in Jesus’ name. And yet they are strangers to him. Their impressive works were built on sand, because they were never founded on a real, saving relationship with Christ himself.

This is the final, most searching application of the whole sermon. It is possible to do much in Jesus’ name and never know him. It is possible to have an outwardly impressive religious life and be building on the sand of your own works. The dividing line is not the quantity of religious activity but whether Christ knows you — whether you have come, empty-handed, through the narrow gate, and rested your whole weight on him. The terror of I never knew you should drive every man to ask the only question that matters: not how much have I done, but do I belong to Christ?

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Hearing and Doing
paras: Jesus says the wise man is the one who hears these words and does them. At first this might sound like a return to works — as if, after all, salvation comes down to performance. But read in the light of the whole sermon, the doing Jesus calls for is precisely the response the sermon has been demanding all along: to stop trusting yourself and come to Christ. The first and deepest act of obedience to this sermon is to receive its verdict — that you cannot — and to flee to the One who can. To hear and not do is to admire the sermon while never letting it drive you to Christ. To hear and do is to let it land, be undone, and build your life on the Rock.

And the obedience that follows is not the anxious performance of a man trying to save himself, but the grateful response of a man already saved, already on the Rock, whose doing flows from grace rather than toward it. The man founded on Christ does obey — the sermon bears fruit in his life — but his obedience is the fruit of his foundation, not the foundation itself. He builds on the Rock, and then he lives like a man whose house is secure, because it is. Hearing and doing, rightly understood, is the whole movement of this study: see your need, come to Christ, and live as one whose house will stand.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Christ the Rock, the Only Foundation
paras: The parable speaks of building on the rock, and Scripture leaves no doubt who the Rock is. “For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” He is the stone the builders rejected that has become the cornerstone, the rock of your salvation, the foundation on which the whole household of God is built. To build on the rock is to build on Christ — on his finished work, his perfect righteousness, his death and resurrection — rather than on the sand of your own performance. The wise man is simply the man who has rested his entire weight on Jesus.

And this is the answer to the verse that began everything. The righteousness that surpasses the scribes and Pharisees — the righteousness without which no man enters the kingdom — is found nowhere in yourself and entirely in Christ. He is the Rock because he is the righteousness. The man founded on him stands not because his house is impressive but because his foundation is unshakable. When the storms of life batter him, he holds. When the final storm of judgment comes, he holds. Not because of what he built, but because of what he built on. Christ the Rock does not fail, and neither does the house founded on him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: From Dust to the Rock That Holds
paras: Psalm 119:25 has anchored this entire study: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). You began with a soul flat on the ground, and the word has done exactly what it promised — it has revived you, not by improving the dust, but by lifting your eyes off yourself and onto Christ. From the dust you have looked up, week by week, to the righteousness that surpasses, to the blessing on the bankrupt, to the heart Christ cleanses, to the love you cannot manufacture, to the Father who sees in secret, to the treasure that lasts, to the care of the Father, to mercy, to the open door — and now, at last, to the Rock that holds. The man clinging to the dust has been pointed, all along, to a foundation that cannot be shaken.

So here, at the end, is the final turn of the whole study: from dust to the Rock. Not a man who has finally cleaned himself up and built an impressive house, but a man who has stopped building on the sand of his own righteousness and rested his entire weight on Christ. The storms will come — they come to every house. But the man founded on the Rock will not fall, because his foundation is not himself but the One who fulfilled this whole sermon in his place. The study is ending, but you are not being sent back to climb the mountain. You are being sent out to live as a man whose house is built on the Rock that holds, from dust to revival, from dust to the Rock, all the way home.

stations.verse: Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.
stations.question: Two houses, one storm, two foundations. When I am honest, what is my house actually built on — Christ, or my own righteousness?
stations.gloss: foundation, the base on which everything rests
stations.live: Inspect your foundation, not your house. Ask not how impressive your life looks, but what it actually rests on — and dig down to the Rock of Christ.
body: Themelion is the foundation — the hidden base that determines whether everything above it stands or falls. It is invisible in fair weather and decisive in the storm. Paul says no other themelion can be laid than Jesus Christ. The whole parable turns on this unseen thing: not the size or beauty of the house, but what it rests on. A life built on the foundation of Christ’s finished work stands when everything is shaken; a life built on self collapses when tested.

stations.verse: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’
stations.question: These are deeply religious people Jesus never knew. Is my hope in what I have done in his name, or in whether he knows me?
stations.gloss: to know, with the knowledge of personal relationship
stations.live: Rest your hope not on your record of works but on belonging to Christ. Ask not “Have I done enough?” but “Does the Shepherd know me as his own?”
body: Ginōskō is not knowledge about a fact but knowledge of a person — the intimate, relational knowing of those who belong to one another. When Jesus says “I never knew you,” he does not mean he lacked information; he means there was no relationship, no belonging. The dividing line on the last day is not religious achievement but whether Christ knows you as his own. The same word describes the Good Shepherd who knows his sheep, and is known by them.

stations.verse: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.
stations.question: There is only one possible foundation, and it is Christ. What else have I been quietly trying to lay underneath my life?

stations.verse: Yahweh is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge; my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower.
stations.question: God himself is called my rock and refuge. In the last storm I faced, did I take refuge in him — or scramble to save myself?
stations.gloss: crag, cliff, rock; a place of security
stations.live: The next time the storm hits this week, do not scramble to reinforce the walls. Climb onto the Rock. Pray Psalm 18:2 out loud.
body: Selaʿ is the high crag — the cliff face a hunted man climbs to when there is nowhere else to go. David knew those rocks; while Saul hunted him, he “went down to the rock” in the wilderness of Maon. So when he sings “Yahweh is my rock,” he is not reaching for a pretty picture. He is naming the one place the enemy could not reach him. The house in the parable is built on rock. David hid in it. Both are saying the same thing: the safety is in what you stand on, not in what you build.

stations.verse: He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’ There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!
stations.question: The rejected stone became the cornerstone, and there is no salvation in any other. Have I built on him, or on a stone of my own choosing?
stations.gloss: cornerstone, the stone that aligns the whole building
stations.live: Let Christ be the cornerstone that aligns everything else — your work, your home, your hopes. A life squared to him stands true; a life squared to anything else runs crooked.
body: Akrogōniaios is the cornerstone — the first and chief stone, set at the corner, from which every other stone and the alignment of the whole building is determined. Christ is this stone: rejected by the builders, yet made the very foundation and standard of the entire structure. Everything in a life is either aligned to him or out of true. To build on the Rock is to set Christ as the cornerstone from which all the rest of life takes its measure.

stations.verse: When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.
stations.question: Jesus taught with an authority the scribes never had. Do I receive his words as the authoritative voice that orders my life, or as good advice to consider?

stations.verse: For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be disappointed.
stations.question: The one who builds on Christ will never be put to shame. Where do I still fear that resting wholly on him will leave me exposed?

stations.verse: For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
stations.question: The whole study sits in one verse: his righteousness for my sin. Have I truly received it, and am I resting my entire weight on it?

stations.verse: Now to him who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy, to God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen.
stations.question: He is able to keep me from stumbling and present me faultless. As this study ends, will I entrust the whole road ahead to the One strong enough to bring me home?
stations.gloss: without stumbling, sure-footed
stations.live: As this study ends, do not trust your footing. Trust the One who is able to keep you on your feet, all the way home.
body: This is the only time the word appears in the New Testament: sure-footed, not stumbling. Picture a narrow mountain trail, loose rock underfoot, a long drop on one side. Jude does not say you are sure-footed. He says God is able to keep you so. The man who finished this sermon knowing he could never climb the mountain is not left to walk the road home on his own feet. The One who kept the whole sermon keeps you on the path.
pulls: The man founded on the Rock will not fall — not because of what he built, but because of what he built on.

practices.title: INSPECT YOUR FOUNDATION, NOT YOUR HOUSE
practices.body: The two houses looked alike until the storm; the difference was the hidden foundation. This week, stop assessing how impressive your life looks and ask the only question that matters: what is it actually built on? Be honest about where you have been resting your weight — your morality, your religious activity, your record — and write it down. Then preach the truth over it: no other foundation can be laid than Jesus Christ. Dig down past the appearance to the Rock.

practices.title: SETTLE WHETHER CHRIST KNOWS YOU
practices.body: The most sobering words in the sermon are “I never knew you,” spoken to busy religious people. This week, move your hope off your works and onto your belonging. Stop asking “Have I done enough?” and start resting in “Christ knows me as his own.” If you have never consciously come to him empty-handed and rested your whole weight on him, do it now: “Lord, I stop trusting what I have done. I come to you, and I rest on you alone.”

practices.title: BUILD BY HEARING AND DOING — IN THAT ORDER
practices.body: The wise man hears and does, and the first act of obedience is to come to Christ. This week, take the words of this sermon that exposed you most and do the deepest thing they require: bring them to Christ and rest on him. Then let real obedience follow as fruit, not foundation — obeying from the security of the Rock, not to earn a place on it. Pray it: “Lord, I build on you first, and then I follow you, as a man whose house is already secure.”

practices.title: LET THE FATHER, SON, AND SPIRIT CARRY YOU THROUGH THE STORMS
practices.body: Storms come to every house; the founded man is not spared them but held through them. This week, when a storm hits — trouble, grief, fear, failure — do not scramble to save yourself. Rest on the Rock: “Father, you chose me; Son, you are my foundation and my righteousness; Spirit, hold me fast.” The Triune God who began this work will keep you and present you faultless. You are not carrying yourself home; he is carrying you.

practices.title: HAND THE ROCK TO ANOTHER MAN
practices.body: You have spent twelve weeks being driven off yourself and onto Christ. Do not keep it to yourself. Before this study ends, sit down with one man still building on the sand of his own righteousness and hand him what you have been given: tell him about the righteousness that surpasses, the narrow gate, the Rock that holds. A man who has been lifted from the dust and set on the Rock is meant to reach back and point another to the same foundation.

title: The House on the Rock
subtitle: from dust to the rock that holds
keyVerse: Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.

passage.text: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?
Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit.
A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.
Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down, and thrown into the fire.
Therefore by their fruits you will know them.
Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.
Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’
Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’
“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.
Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.”
When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching,
for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. This is where the whole study has been heading. Let each verse land before you answer — and where a Greek or Hebrew word is opened, let it sharpen what you are praying over.
lifeIntro: This is the last week, so let the application reach past these seven days and into the rest of the road. The whole study comes down to this: stop building on the sand of your own righteousness, and rest your entire life on Christ the Rock.

bottomLine: Matthew 7:24–29 ends the sermon as it must end — with a call to respond. Two men build two houses that look alike until the storm reveals the hidden foundation, and only the house on the rock stands. The terror of “I never knew you” warns that impressive religious works built on the sand of self will collapse, while the one Christ knows stands secure. To hear and do is to let the sermon land, be undone, and build your whole life on Christ the Rock — the only foundation, the rejected stone become the cornerstone, the surpassing righteousness without which no man enters the kingdom. The study ends not by sending you back to climb the mountain, but by sending you out to live as a man whose house is founded on the Rock that holds, from dust to revival, from dust to the Rock, all the way home.
benediction: Brother, twelve weeks ago you began with a soul face down in the dust, praying the prayer of Psalm 119:25: “My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word” (NKJV). And week by week, the word has done exactly what it promised — it has revived you, not by improving the dust, but by lifting your eyes off yourself and onto Christ. You have looked up to the righteousness that surpasses, to the blessing on the bankrupt, to the heart Christ cleanses, to the love you cannot manufacture, to the Father who sees in secret, to the treasure that lasts, to the care of the Father, to mercy, to the open door — and now, at the end of the road, to the Rock that holds.

This was always where the sermon was going. Every demand that exposed you, every standard you could not reach, every mirror that undid you — all of it was driving you here, to the foundation. And the foundation has a name. The righteousness that surpasses the scribes and Pharisees, without which no man enters the kingdom, was never going to be found in you. It is found wholly in Christ, the Rock, who fulfilled this entire sermon in your place — who never sinned in heart or word, who loved his enemies perfectly, who was perfect as the Father is perfect — and who became sin for you so that in him you might become the righteousness of God. He is the cornerstone the builders rejected, and he has become the only foundation that holds.

So lift up your eyes one last time, and keep them lifted long after this study ends. When the storms of this life beat against your house, lift up your eyes — you are founded on the Rock, and you will not fall. When you fail again and the dust says you were never really his, lift up your eyes — your hope was never your house, but your foundation. When the final storm of judgment looms, lift up your eyes to the One “who is able to keep them from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy.” The study is over, but the walk is just beginning. You know the righteousness now. You know the Rock. So get up off the dust, lift up your eyes, and walk the rest of the road home — built on Christ, the Rock that holds, from dust to glory, every step of the way.
closingVerse: Your soul once clung to the dust. Lift up your eyes — your house is built on Christ the Rock, and it will not fall, all the way home.
carry: The study is ending, but the road is not. Where is the Spirit inviting you to keep building your whole life on Christ the Rock — and who will you take with you, and point to the same foundation?
